entries.c59dd6d323527469145defc63164af58bda014c2: <div sID="gen31600" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="11" osisID="2Cor.11" sID="2Cor.11"/> <div eID="gen31600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31601" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31602" type="x-p"/> In this chapter the apostle goes on with his discourse, in opposition to the false apostles, who were very industrious to lessen his interest and reputation among the Corinthians, and had prevailed too much by their insinuations. I. He apologizes for going about to commend himself, and gives the reason for what he did, <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.1-2Cor.11.4">ver. 1-4</reference>. II. He mentions, in his own necessary vindication, his equality with the other apostles, and with the false apostles in this particular of preaching the gospel to the Corinthians freely, without wages, <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.5-2Cor.11.15">ver. 5-15</reference>. III. He makes another preface to what he was about further to say in his own justification, <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.16-2Cor.11.21">ver. 16-21</reference>. And, IV. He gives a large account of his qualifications, labours, and sufferings, in which he exceeded the false apostles, <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.22-2Cor.11.33">ver. 22, to the end</reference>.
entries.3c8a7f0ec8587616cc4e11fd731946beeded47c8: <div eID="gen31602" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31601" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Apostle Asserts His Claims. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 57.)</title> <div sID="gen31603" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Would to God ye could bear with me a little in <hi type="italic">my</hi> folly: and indeed bear with me. <hi type="super">2</hi> For I am jealous over you with godly jealousy: for I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present <hi type="italic">you as</hi> a chaste virgin to Christ. <hi type="super">3</hi> But I fear, lest by any means, as the serpent beguiled Eve through his subtilty, so your minds should be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ. <hi type="super">4</hi> For if he that cometh preacheth another Jesus, whom we have not preached, or <hi type="italic">if</hi> ye receive another spirit, which ye have not received, or another gospel, which ye have not accepted, ye might well bear with <hi type="italic">him.</hi> <div eID="gen31603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31604" type="x-p"/> Here we may observe, 1. The apology the apostle makes for going about to commend himself. He is loth to enter upon this subject of self-commendation: <hi type="italic">Would to God you could bear with me a little in my folly,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.1">v. 1</reference>. He calls this folly, because too often it is really no better. In his case it was necessary; yet, seeing others might apprehend it to be folly in him, he desires them to bear with it. Note, As much against the grain as it is with a proud man to acknowledge his infirmities, so much is it against the grain with a humble man to speak in his own praise. It is no pleasure to a good man to speak well of himself, yet in some cases it is lawful, namely, when it is for the advantage of others, or for our own necessary vindication; as thus it was here. For, 2. We have the reasons for what the apostle did. (1.) To preserve the Corinthians from being corrupted by the insinuations of the false apostles, <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.2-2Cor.11.3">v. 2, 3</reference>. He tells them <hi type="italic">he was jealous over them with godly jealousy;</hi> he was afraid lest their faith should be weakened by hearkening to such suggestions as tended to lessen their regard to his ministry, by which they were brought to the Christian faith. He had <hi type="italic">espoused them to one husband,</hi> that is, converted them to Christianity (and the conversion of a soul is its marriage to the Lord Jesus); and he was desirous to <hi type="italic">present them as a chaste virgin</hi>—pure, and spotless, and faithful, not having <hi type="italic">their minds corrupted</hi> with false doctrines by false teachers, as <hi type="italic">Eve was beguiled by the subtlety of the serpent.</hi> This godly jealousy in the apostle was a mixture of love and fear; and faithful ministers cannot but be afraid and concerned for their people, lest they should lose that which they have received, and turn from what they have embraced, especially when <hi type="italic">deceivers have gone abroad,</hi> or have <hi type="italic">crept in among them.</hi> (2.) To vindicate himself against the false apostles, forasmuch as they could not pretend they had another Jesus, or another Spirit, or another gospel, to preach to them, <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.4">v. 4</reference>. If this had been the case, there would have been some colour of reason to bear with them, or to hearken to them. But seeing there is but one Jesus, one Spirit, and one gospel, that is, or at least that ought to be, preached to them and received by them, what reason could there be why the Corinthians should be prejudiced against him, who first converted them to the faith, by the artifices of any adversary? It was a just occasion of jealousy that such persons designed to preach another Jesus, another Spirit, and another gospel.
entries.544b592607cf7db9656543ca993e111dd9328fb3: <div eID="gen31604" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Apostle Asserts His Claims. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 57.)</title> <div sID="gen31605" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> For I suppose I was not a whit behind the very chiefest apostles. <hi type="super">6</hi> But though <hi type="italic">I be</hi> rude in speech, yet not in knowledge; but we have been thoroughly made manifest among you in all things. <hi type="super">7</hi> Have I committed an offence in abasing myself that ye might be exalted, because I have preached to you the gospel of God freely? <hi type="super">8</hi> I robbed other churches, taking wages <hi type="italic">of them,</hi> to do you service. <hi type="super">9</hi> And when I was present with you, and wanted, I was chargeable to no man: for that which was lacking to me the brethren which came from Macedonia supplied: and in all <hi type="italic">things</hi> I have kept myself from being burdensome unto you, and <hi type="italic">so</hi> will I keep <hi type="italic">myself.</hi> 10 As the truth of Christ is in me, no man shall stop me of this boasting in the regions of Achaia. <hi type="super">11</hi> Wherefore? because I love you not? God knoweth. <hi type="super">12</hi> But what I do, that I will do, that I may cut off occasion from them which desire occasion; that wherein they glory, they may be found even as we. 13 For such <hi type="italic">are</hi> false apostles, deceitful workers, transforming themselves into the apostles of Christ. <hi type="super">14</hi> And no marvel; for Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light. 15 Therefore <hi type="italic">it is</hi> no great thing if his ministers also be transformed as the ministers of righteousness; whose end shall be according to their works. <div eID="gen31605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31606" type="x-p"/> After the foregoing preface to what he was about to say, the apostle in these verses mentions, <div eID="gen31606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31607" type="x-p"/> I. His equality with the other apostles—that <hi type="italic">he was not a whit behind the very chief of the apostles,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.5">v. 5</reference>. This he expresses very modestly: <hi type="italic">I suppose so.</hi> He might have spoken very positively. The apostleship, as an office, was equal in all the apostles; but the apostles, like other Christians, differed one from another. These <hi type="italic">stars differed one from another in glory,</hi> and Paul was indeed of the first magnitude; yet he speaks modestly of himself, and humbly owns his personal infirmity, that he was <hi type="italic">rude in speech,</hi> had not such a graceful delivery as some others might have. Some think that he was a man of very low stature, and that his voice was proportionably small; others think that he may have had some impediment in his speech, perhaps a stammering tongue. However, he was not rude <hi type="italic">in knowledge;</hi> he was not unacquainted with the best rules of oratory and the art of persuasion, much less was he ignorant of the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, as had been <hi type="italic">thoroughly manifested among them.</hi> <div eID="gen31607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31608" type="x-p"/> II. His equality with the false apostles in this particular—the preaching of the gospel unto them freely, without wages. This the apostle largely insists on, and shows that, as they could not but own him to be a minister of Christ, so they ought to acknowledge he had been a good friend to them. For, 1. He had preached the gospel to them freely, <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.7-2Cor.11.10">v. 7-10</reference>. He had proved at large, in his former epistle to them, the lawfulness of ministers' receiving maintenance from the people, and the duty of the people to give them an honourable maintenance; and here he says he himself had <hi type="italic">taken wages of other churches</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.8">v. 8</reference>), so that he had a right to have asked and received from them: yet he waived his right, and chose rather to abase himself, by working with his hands in the trade of tent-making to maintain himself, than be burdensome to them, that they might <hi type="italic">be exalted,</hi> or encouraged to receive the gospel, which they had so cheaply; yea, he chose rather to be supplied from Macedonia than to be chargeable unto them. 2. He informs them of the reason of this his conduct among them. It was not because <hi type="italic">he did not love them</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.11">v. 11</reference>), or was unwilling to receive tokens of their love (for love and friendship are manifested by mutual giving and receiving), but it was to avoid offence, that <hi type="italic">he might cut off occasion from those that desired occasion.</hi> He would not give occasion for any to accuse him of worldly designs in preaching the gospel, or that he intended to make a trade of it, to enrich himself; and that others who opposed him at Corinth might not in this respect gain an advantage against him: that wherein <hi type="italic">they gloried,</hi> as to this matter, <hi type="italic">they might be found even as he,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.12">v. 12</reference>. It is not improbable to suppose that the chief of the false teachers at Corinth, or some among them, were rich, and taught (or deceived) the people freely, and might accuse the apostle or his fellow-labourers as mercenary men, who received hire or wages, and therefore the apostle kept to his resolution not to be chargeable to any of the Corinthians. <div eID="gen31608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31609" type="x-p"/> III. The false apostles are charged <hi type="italic">as deceitful workers</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.13">v. 13</reference>), and that upon this account, because they would <hi type="italic">transform themselves</hi> into the likeness of the apostles of Christ, and, though they were the ministers of Satan, would seem to be the <hi type="italic">ministers of righteousness.</hi> They would be as industrious and as generous in promoting error as the apostles were in preaching truth; they would endeavour as much to undermine the kingdom of Christ as the apostles did to establish it. There were counterfeit prophets under the Old Testament, who wore the garb and learned the language of the prophets of the Lord. So there were counterfeit apostles under the New Testament, who seemed in many respects like the true apostles of Christ. And no marvel (says the apostle); hypocrisy is a thing not to be much wondered at in this world, especially when we consider the great influence Satan has upon the minds of many, who <hi type="italic">rules in the hearts of the children of disobedience.</hi> As he can turn himself into any shape, and put on almost any form, and look sometimes <hi type="italic">like an angel of light,</hi> in order to promote his kingdom of darkness, so he will teach his ministers and instruments to do the same. But it follows, <hi type="italic">Their end is according to their works</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.15">v. 15</reference>); the end will discover them to be deceitful workers, and their work will end in ruin and destruction.
entries.21fe7c15a02e6719706d27fbf27a59be49bdd737: <div eID="gen31609" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Apostle Asserts His Claims. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 57.)</title> <div sID="gen31610" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> I say again, Let no man think me a fool; if otherwise, yet as a fool receive me, that I may boast myself a little. <hi type="super">17</hi> That which I speak, I speak <hi type="italic">it</hi> not after the Lord, but as it were foolishly, in this confidence of boasting. 18 Seeing that many glory after the flesh, I will glory also. <hi type="super">19</hi> For ye suffer fools gladly, seeing ye <hi type="italic">yourselves</hi> are wise. <hi type="super">20</hi> For ye suffer, if a man bring you into bondage, if a man devour <hi type="italic">you,</hi> if a man take <hi type="italic">of you,</hi> if a man exalt himself, if a man smite you on the face. 21 I speak as concerning reproach, as though we had been weak. Howbeit whereinsoever any is bold, (I speak foolishly,) I am bold also. <div eID="gen31610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31611" type="x-p"/> Here we have a further excuse that the apostle makes for what he was about to say in his own vindication. 1. He would not have them think he was guilty of folly, in saying what he said to vindicate himself: <hi type="italic">Let no man think me a fool,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.16">v. 16</reference>. Ordinarily, indeed, it is unbecoming a wise man to be much and often speaking in his own praise. Boasting of ourselves is usually not only a sign of a proud mind, but a mark of folly also. However, says the apostle, yet <hi type="italic">as a fool receive me;</hi> that is, if you count it folly in me to <hi type="italic">boast a little,</hi> yet give due regard to what I shall say. 2. He mentions a caution, to prevent the abuse of what he should say, telling them that what he spoke, <hi type="italic">he did not speak after the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.17">v. 17</reference>. He would not have them think that boasting of ourselves, or glorying in what we have, is a thing commanded by the Lord in general unto Christians, nor yet that this is always necessary in our own vindication; though it may be lawfully used, because not contrary to the Lord, when, strictly speaking, it is not after the Lord. It is the duty and practice of Christians, in obedience to the command and example of the Lord, rather to humble and abase themselves; yet prudence must direct in what circumstances it is needful to do that which we may do lawfully, even speak of what God has wrought for us, and in us, and by us too. 3. He gives a good reason why they should suffer him to boast a little; namely, because they suffered others to do so who had less reason. <hi type="italic">Seeing many glory after the flesh</hi> (of carnal privileges, or outward advantages and attainments), <hi type="italic">I will glory also,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.18">v. 18</reference>. But he would not glory in those things, though he had as much or more reason than others to do so. But he gloried in his infirmities, as he tells them afterwards. The Corinthians thought themselves wise, and might think it an instance of wisdom to bear with the weakness of others, and therefore suffered others to do what might seem folly; therefore the apostle would have them bear with him. Or these words, <hi type="italic">You suffer fools gladly, seeing you yourselves are wise</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.19">v. 19</reference>), may be ironical, and then the meaning is this: "Notwithstanding all your wisdom, you willingly suffer yourselves to be <hi type="italic">brought into bondage</hi> under the Jewish yoke, or suffer others to tyrannize over you; nay, to <hi type="italic">devour you,</hi> or make a prey of you, and <hi type="italic">take of you</hi> hire for their own advantage, and to <hi type="italic">exalt themselves</hi> above you, and lord it over you; nay, even to <hi type="italic">smite you on the face,</hi> or impose upon you to your very faces (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.20">v. 20</reference>), upbraiding you while they reproach me, as if you had been very weak in showing regard to me," <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.21">v. 21</reference>. Seeing this was the case, that the Corinthians, or some among them, could so easily bear all this from the false apostles, it was reasonable for the apostle to desire, and expect, they should bear with what might seem to them an indiscretion in him, seeing the circumstances of the case were such as made it needful that <hi type="italic">whereinsoever any were bold</hi> he should be <hi type="italic">bold also,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.21">v. 21</reference>.
entries.bdec9ff5afe0baa0b1007d38921e06af608c27ae: <div eID="gen31611" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Apostle Recounts His Sufferings. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 57.)</title> <div sID="gen31612" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">22</hi> Are they Hebrews? so <hi type="italic">am</hi> I. Are they Israelites? so <hi type="italic">am</hi> I. Are they the seed of Abraham? so <hi type="italic">am</hi> I. <hi type="super">23</hi> Are they ministers of Christ? (I speak as a fool) I <hi type="italic">am</hi> more; in labours more abundant, in stripes above measure, in prisons more frequent, in deaths oft. <hi type="super">24</hi> Of the Jews five times received I forty <hi type="italic">stripes</hi> save one. <hi type="super">25</hi> Thrice was I beaten with rods, once was I stoned, thrice I suffered shipwreck, a night and a day I have been in the deep; 26 <hi type="italic">In</hi> journeyings often, <hi type="italic">in</hi> perils of waters, <hi type="italic">in</hi> perils of robbers, <hi type="italic">in</hi> perils by <hi type="italic">mine own</hi> countrymen, <hi type="italic">in</hi> perils by the heathen, <hi type="italic">in</hi> perils in the city, <hi type="italic">in</hi> perils in the wilderness, <hi type="italic">in</hi> perils in the sea, <hi type="italic">in</hi> perils among false brethren; <hi type="super">27</hi> In weariness and painfulness, in watchings often, in hunger and thirst, in fastings often, in cold and nakedness. <hi type="super">28</hi> Beside those things that are without, that which cometh upon me daily, the care of all the churches. <hi type="super">29</hi> Who is weak, and I am not weak? who is offended, and I burn not? <hi type="super">30</hi> If I must needs glory, I will glory of the things which concern mine infirmities. <hi type="super">31</hi> The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, which is blessed for evermore, knoweth that I lie not. <hi type="super">32</hi> In Damascus the governor under Aretas the king kept the city of the Damascenes with a garrison, desirous to apprehend me: <hi type="super">33</hi> And through a window in a basket was I let down by the wall, and escaped his hands. <div eID="gen31612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31613" type="x-p"/> Here the apostle gives a large account of his own qualifications, labours, and sufferings (not out of pride or vain-glory, but to the honour of God, who had enabled him to do and suffer so much for the cause of Christ), and wherein he excelled the false apostles, who would lessen his character and usefulness among the Corinthians. Observe, <div eID="gen31613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31614" type="x-p"/> I. He mentions the privileges of his birth (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.22">v. 22</reference>), which were equal to any they could pretend to. He was a Hebrew of the Hebrews; of a family among the Jews that never intermarried with the Gentiles. He was also an Israelite, and could boast of his being descended from the beloved Jacob as well as they, and was also of the seed of Abraham, and not of the proselytes. It should seem from this that the false apostles were of the Jewish race, who gave disturbance to the Gentile converts. <div eID="gen31614" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31615" type="x-p"/> II. He makes mention also of his apostleship, that he was more than an ordinary minister of Christ, <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.23">v. 23</reference>. God had counted him faithful, and had put him into the ministry. He had been a useful minister of Christ unto them; they had found full proofs of his ministry: <hi type="italic">Are they ministers of Christ? I am more so.</hi> <div eID="gen31615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31616" type="x-p"/> III. He chiefly insists upon this, that he had been an extraordinary sufferer for Christ; and this was what he gloried in, or rather he gloried in the grace of God that had enabled him to be more <hi type="italic">abundant in labours,</hi> and to endure very great sufferings, such as <hi type="italic">stripes above measure, frequent imprisonments,</hi> and <hi type="italic">often</hi> the dangers of <hi type="italic">death,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.23">v. 23</reference>. Note, When the apostle would prove himself an extraordinary minister, he proves that he had been an extraordinary sufferer. Paul was the apostle of the Gentiles, and for that reason was hated of the Jews. They did all they could against him; and among the Gentiles also he met with hard usage. Bonds and imprisonments were familiar to him; never was the most notorious malefactor more frequently in the hands of public justice than Paul was for righteousness' sake. The jail and the whipping-post, and all other hard usages of those who are accounted the worst of men, were what he was accustomed to. As to the Jews, whenever he fell into their hands, they never spared him. <hi type="italic">Five times</hi> he fell under their lash, and received <hi type="italic">forty stripes save one,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.24">v. 24</reference>. Forty stripes was the utmost their law allowed (<reference osisRef="Deut.25.3">Deut. xxv. 3</reference>), but it was usual with them, that they might not exceed, to abate one at least of that number. And to have the abatement of one only was all the favour that ever Paul received from them. The Gentiles were not tied up to that moderation, and among them <hi type="italic">he was thrice beaten with rods,</hi> of which we may suppose once was at Philippi, <reference osisRef="Acts.16.22">Acts xvi. 22</reference>. <hi type="italic">Once he was stoned</hi> in a popular tumult, and was taken up for dead, <reference osisRef="Acts.14.19">Acts xiv. 19</reference>. He says that <hi type="italic">thrice he suffered shipwreck;</hi> and we may believe him, though the sacred history gives a relation but of one. <hi type="italic">A night and a day he had been in the deep</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.25">v. 25</reference>), in some deep dungeon or other, shut up as a prisoner. Thus he was all his days a constant confessor; perhaps scarcely a year of his life, after his conversion, passed without suffering some hardship or other for his religion; yet this was not all, for, wherever he went, he went in perils; he was exposed to perils of all sorts. If he journeyed by land, or voyaged by sea, he was in perils of robbers, or enemies of some sort; the Jews, his own countrymen, sought to kill him, or do him a mischief; the heathen, to whom he was sent, were not more kind to him, for among them he was in peril. If he was in the city, or in the wilderness, still he was in peril. He was in peril not only among avowed enemies, but among those also who called themselves brethren, but were false brethren, <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.26">v. 26</reference>. Besides all this, he had great weariness and painfulness in his ministerial labours, and these are things that will come into account shortly, and people will be reckoned with for all the care and pains of their ministers concerning them. Paul was a stranger to wealth and plenty, power and pleasure, preferment and ease; he was in <hi type="italic">watchings often,</hi> and exposed to <hi type="italic">hunger and thirst;</hi> in <hi type="italic">fastings often,</hi> it may be out of necessity; and endured <hi type="italic">cold and nakedness,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.27">v. 27</reference>. Thus was he, who was one of the greatest blessings of the age, used as if he had been the burden of the earth, and the plague of his generation. And yet this is not all; for, as an apostle, the <hi type="italic">care of all the churches</hi> lay on him, <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.28">v. 28</reference>. He mentions this last, as if this lay the heaviest upon him, and as if he could better bear all the persecutions of his enemies than the scandals that were to be found in the churches he had the oversight of. <hi type="italic">Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is offended, and I burn not?</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.29">v. 29</reference>. There was not a weak Christian with whom he did not sympathize, nor any one scandalized, but he was affected therewith. See what little reason we have to be in love with the pomp and plenty of this world, when this blessed apostle, one of the best of men that ever lived, excepting Jesus Christ, felt so much hardship in it. Nor was he ashamed of all this, but, on the contrary, it was what he accounted his honour; and therefore, much against the grain as it was with him to glory, yet, says he, <hi type="italic">if I must needs glory,</hi> if my adversaries will oblige me to it in my own necessary vindication, <hi type="italic">I will glory in these my infirmities,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.30">v. 30</reference>. Note, Sufferings for righteousness' sake will, the most of any thing, redound to our honour. <div eID="gen31616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31617" type="x-p"/> In the <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.32-2Cor.11.33">last two verses</reference>, he mentions one particular part of his sufferings out of its place, as if he had forgotten it before, or because the deliverance God wrought for him was most remarkable; namely, the danger he was in at Damascus, soon after he was converted, and not settled in Christianity, at least in the ministry and apostleship. This is recorded, <reference osisRef="Acts.9.24-Acts.9.25">Acts ix. 24, 25</reference>. This was his first great danger and difficulty, and the rest of his life was a piece with this. And it is observable that, lest it should be thought he spoke more than was true, the apostle confirms this narrative with a solemn oath, or appeal to the omniscience of God, <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.31">v. 31</reference>. It is a great comfort to a good man that <hi type="italic">the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ,</hi> who is an omniscient God, knows the truth of all he says, and knows all he does and all he suffers for his sake.  <chapter eID="2Cor.11"/> <div eID="gen31617" type="x-p"/>

entries.931342a94dd155b70e5fca03a6ee5bd96e4f0799: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17357"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 11</title> <div sID="gen34638" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.1-2Cor.11.33">2Co 11:1-33</reference>. Through Jealousy over the Corinthians, Who Made More Account of the False Apostles Than of Him, He Is Obliged to Commend Himself as in Many Respects Superior.<div eID="gen34638" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34639" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17357"/><hi type="bold">1. Would to God--</hi>Translate as Greek, "I would that."<div eID="gen34639" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34640" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bear with me--</hi>I may ask not unreasonably to be borne with; not so the false apostles (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.4">2Co 11:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.20">20</reference>).<div eID="gen34640" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34641" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my--</hi>not in the oldest manuscripts.<div eID="gen34641" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34642" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">folly--</hi>The Greek is a milder term than that for "foolishness" in <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.19">1Co 3:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.5.22">Mt 5:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.25.2">25:2</reference>. The Greek for "folly" here implies imprudence; the Greek for "foolishness" includes the idea of perversity and wickedness.<div eID="gen34642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34643" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and indeed bear--</hi>A request (so <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.16">2Co 11:16</reference>). But the Greek and the sense favor the translation, "But indeed (I need not wish it, for) ye do bear with me"; still I wish you to bear with me further, while I enter at large into self-commendations. <div eID="gen34643" type="x-p"/>
entries.24cedbd51808fab80a60767df3da5952082a5a6d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17358"/><div sID="gen34644" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17358"/><hi type="bold">2. For I am jealous--</hi>The justification of his self-commendations lies in his zealous care lest they should fall from Christ, to whom he, as "the friend of the Bridegroom" (<reference osisRef="John.3.29">Joh 3:29</reference>), has espoused them; in order to lead them back from the false apostles to Christ, he is obliged to boast as an apostle of Christ, in a way which, but for the motive, would be "folly."<div eID="gen34644" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34645" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">godly jealousy--</hi>literally, "jealousy of God" (compare <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.12">2Co 1:12</reference>, "godly sincerity," literally, "sincerity of God"). "If I am immoderate, I am immoderate to God" [Bengel]. A jealousy which has God's honor at heart (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.19.10">1Ki 19:10</reference>).<div eID="gen34645" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34646" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I ... espoused you--</hi>Paul uses a Greek term applied properly to the bridegroom, just as he ascribes to himself "jealousy," a feeling properly belonging to the husband; so entirely does he identify himself with Christ.<div eID="gen34646" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34647" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">present you as a chaste virgin to Christ--</hi>at His coming, when the heavenly marriage shall take place (<reference osisRef="Matt.25.6">Mt 25:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.19.7">Re 19:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.19.9">9</reference>). What Paul here says he desires to do, namely, "present" the Church as "a chaste virgin" to Christ, Christ Himself is said to do in the fuller sense. Whatever ministers do effectively, is really done by Christ (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.27-Eph.5.32">Ep 5:27-32</reference>). The espousals are going on now. He does not say "chaste virgins"; for not individual members, but the whole body of believers conjointly constitute the Bride. <div eID="gen34647" type="x-p"/>
entries.632171f8c5c21cbaf8344f1c858880181da8e8ca: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17359"/><div sID="gen34648" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17359"/><hi type="bold">3. I fear--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Cor.12.20">2Co 12:20</reference>); not inconsistent with love. His source of fear was their yielding character.<div eID="gen34648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34649" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">subtilty--</hi>the utter foe of the "simplicity" which is intent on ONE object, Jesus, and seeks none "other," and no "other" and different Spirit (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.4">2Co 11:4</reference>); but loves him with tender SINGLENESS OF AFFECTION. Where Eve first gave way, was in mentally harboring for a moment the possibility insinuated by the serpent, of God not having her truest interests at heart, and of this "other" professing friend being more concerned for her than God.<div eID="gen34649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34650" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">corrupted--</hi>so as to lose their virgin purity through seducers (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.4">2Co 11:4</reference>). The same Greek stands for "minds" as for "thoughts" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.10.5">2Co 10:5</reference>, also see on <reference osisRef="2Cor.10.5">2Co 10:5</reference>); intents of the will, or mind. The oldest manuscripts after "simplicity," add, "and the purity" or "chastity."<div eID="gen34650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34651" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in Christ--</hi>rather, "that is towards Christ." <div eID="gen34651" type="x-p"/>
entries.5775320998384670febc10b075e8e3eb1f769aa9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17360"/><div sID="gen34652" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17360"/><hi type="bold">4. if, &c.--</hi>which in fact is impossible. However, if it were possible, ye might then bear with them (see on <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.1">2Co 11:1</reference>). But there can be no new Gospel; there is but the one which I first preached; therefore it ought not to be "borne" by you, that the false teachers should attempt to supersede me.<div eID="gen34652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34653" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he that cometh--</hi>the high-sounding title assumed by the false teachers, who arrogated Christ's own peculiar title (Greek, <reference osisRef="Matt.11.3">Mt 11:3</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Heb.10.37">He 10:37</reference>), "He that is coming." Perhaps he was leader of the party which assumed peculiarly to be "Christ's" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.10.7">2Co 10:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.12">1Co 1:12</reference>); hence his assumption of the title.<div eID="gen34653" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34654" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">preacheth ... receive--</hi>is preaching ... ye are receiving.<div eID="gen34654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34655" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Jesus--</hi>the "Jesus" of Gospel history. He therefore does not say "Christ," which refers to the office.<div eID="gen34655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34656" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">another ... another--</hi>Greek, "another Jesus ... a different Spirit ... a different Gospel." Another implies a distinct individual of the same kind; different implies one quite distinct in kind.<div eID="gen34656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34657" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which ye have not received--</hi>from us.<div eID="gen34657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34658" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">spirit ... received ... gospel ... accepted--</hi>The will of man is passive in RECEIVING the "Spirit"; but it is actively concurrent with the will of God (which goes before to give the good will) in ACCEPTING the "Gospel."<div eID="gen34658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34659" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ye might well bear with him--</hi>There would be an excuse for your conduct, though a bad one (for ye ought to give heed to no Gospel other than what ye have already heard from me, <reference osisRef="Gal.1.6">Ga 1:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.7">7</reference>); but the false teachers do not even pretend they have "another Jesus" and a "different Gospel" to bring before you; they merely try to supplant me, your accredited Teacher. Yet ye not only "bear with" them, but prefer them. <div eID="gen34659" type="x-p"/>
entries.f7cec6bc0de531cf3250d02f4a6f8f700809ac6d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17361"/><div sID="gen34660" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17361"/><hi type="bold">5. For--</hi>My claim is superior to that of the false teachers, "For," &c.<div eID="gen34660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34661" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I suppose--</hi>I reckon [Alford].<div eID="gen34661" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34662" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I was not--</hi>Greek, "That I have not been, and am not."<div eID="gen34662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34663" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the very chiefest apostles--</hi>James, Peter, and John, the witnesses of Christ's transfiguration and agony in Gethsemane. Rather, "those overmuch apostles," those surpassers of the apostles in their own esteem. This sense is proved by the fact that the context contains no comparison between him and the apostles, but only between him and the false teachers; <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.6">2Co 11:6</reference> also alludes to these, and not to the apostles; compare also the parallel phrase, "false apostles" (see on <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.13">2Co 11:13</reference> and <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.11">2Co 12:11</reference>) [Alford]. <div eID="gen34663" type="x-p"/>
entries.3f1999e1f87ee7037f7f624799a6cafe156e315f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17362"/><div sID="gen34664" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17362"/><hi type="bold">6. rude--</hi>Greek, "a common man"; a "laic"; not rhetorically trained; unskilled in finish of diction. 1Co 2:<reference osisRef="1Cor.4.13">1-4, 13</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.10.10">2Co 10:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.10.11">11</reference>, shows his words were not without weight, though his "speech" was deficient in oratorical artifice. "Yet I am not so in my knowledge" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.12.1-2Cor.12.5">2Co 12:1-5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.3.1-Eph.3.5">Ep 3:1-5</reference>).<div eID="gen34664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34665" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">have been ... made manifest--</hi>Read with the oldest manuscripts, "We have made things (Gospel truths) manifest," thus showing our "knowledge." English Version would mean, I leave it to yourselves to decide whether I be rude in speech ... : for we have been thoroughly (literally, "in everything") made manifest among you (literally, "in respect to you"; "in relation to you"). He had not by reserve kept back his "knowledge" in divine mysteries from them (<reference osisRef="2Cor.2.17">2Co 2:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.2">4:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.20.20">Ac 20:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.20.27">27</reference>).<div eID="gen34665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34666" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in all things--</hi>The Greek rather favors the translation, "among all men"; the sense then is, we have manifested the whole truth among all men with a view to your benefit [Alford]. But the Greek in <reference osisRef="Phil.4.12">Php 4:12</reference>, "In each thing and in all things," sanctions English Version, which gives a clearer sense. <div eID="gen34666" type="x-p"/>
entries.e31da7236015e3f065dd697f0b74ac491442d6a2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17363"/><div sID="gen34667" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17363"/><hi type="bold">7. Have I--</hi>literally, "Or have I?" Connected with <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.6">2Co 11:6</reference>, "Or will any of you make it an objection that I have preached to you gratuitously?" He leaves their good feeling to give the answer, that this, so far from being an objection, was a decided superiority in him above the false apostles (<reference osisRef="1Cor.9.6-1Cor.9.15">1Co 9:6-15</reference>).<div eID="gen34667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34668" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">abasing myself--</hi>in my mode of living, waiving my right of maintenance, and earning it by manual labor; perhaps with slaves as his fellow laborers (<reference osisRef="Acts.18.3">Ac 18:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.4.12">Php 4:12</reference>).<div eID="gen34668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34669" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ye ... exalted--</hi>spiritually, by your admission to Gospel privileges.<div eID="gen34669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34670" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">because--</hi>"in that."<div eID="gen34670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34671" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">gospel of God--</hi>"of God" implies its divine glory to which they were admitted.<div eID="gen34671" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34672" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">freely--</hi>"without charge." <div eID="gen34672" type="x-p"/>
entries.65c04f767ab5d34dff43b0369f7dc26bc35dcc49: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17364"/><div sID="gen34673" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17364"/><hi type="bold">8. I robbed--</hi>that is, took from them in order to spare you more than what was their fair share of contribution to my maintenance, for example, the Philippian Church (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.15">Php 4:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Phil.4.16">16</reference>).<div eID="gen34673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34674" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wages--</hi>"subsidy."<div eID="gen34674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34675" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to do you service--</hi>Greek, "with a view to ministration to you"; compare "supplied" (Greek, "in addition"), <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.9">2Co 11:9</reference>, implying, he brought with him from the Macedonians, supplies towards his maintenance at Corinth; and (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.9">2Co 11:9</reference>) when those resources failed ("when I wanted") he received a new supply, while there, from the same source. <div eID="gen34675" type="x-p"/>
entries.918f116a48c9d259255478da087a585711dc9ac9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17365"/><div sID="gen34676" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17365"/><hi type="bold">9. wanted--</hi>"was in want."<div eID="gen34676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34677" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">chargeable--</hi>Greek, "burdensome," literally, "to torpify," and so to oppress. Jerome says it is a Cilician word (<reference osisRef="2Cor.12.14">2Co 12:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.16">16</reference>).<div eID="gen34677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34678" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the brethren which came--</hi>rather, as Greek, "the brethren when they came." Perhaps Timotheus and Silas (<reference osisRef="Acts.8.1">Ac 8:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.8.5">5</reference>). Compare <reference osisRef="Phil.4.15">Php 4:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Phil.4.16">16</reference>, which refers to donations received from the Philippians (who were in Macedonia) at two distinct periods ("once and again"), one at Thessalonica, the other after his departure from Macedonia, that is, when he came into Achaia to Corinth (from the church in which city he would receive no help); and this "in the beginning of the Gospel," that is, at its first preaching in these parts. Thus all three, the two Epistles and history, mutually, and no doubt undesignedly, coincide; a sure test of genuineness.<div eID="gen34678" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34679" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">supplied--</hi>Greek, "supplied in addition," namely, in addition to their former contributions; or as Bengel, in addition to the supply obtained by my own manual labor. <div eID="gen34679" type="x-p"/>
entries.4ff19a0eee6f99e925a6b35bb892225327504733: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17366"/><div sID="gen34680" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17366"/>10. Greek, "There is (the) truth of Christ in me that," &c. (<reference osisRef="Rom.9.1">Ro 9:1</reference>).<div eID="gen34680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34681" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">no man shall stop me of--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read, "This boasting shall not be shut (that is, stopped) as regards me." "Boasting is as it were personified ... shall not have its mouth stopped as regards me" [Alford]. <div eID="gen34681" type="x-p"/>
entries.c0c7fa865b87211e0ed17a971bbc1996925ea2bf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17367"/><div sID="gen34682" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17367"/>11. Love is often offended at its favors being not accepted, as though the party to whom they are offered wished to be under no obligation to the offerer. <div eID="gen34682" type="x-p"/>
entries.433a769696786676eb783f89943529acd2d5afc9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17368"/><div sID="gen34683" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17368"/><hi type="bold">12. I will do--</hi>I will continue to decline help.<div eID="gen34683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34684" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">occasion--</hi>Greek, "the occasion," namely, of misrepresenting my motives, which would be afforded to my detractors, if I accepted help.<div eID="gen34684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34685" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that wherein they glory, they may be found even as we--</hi>Bengel joins this clause with "the occasion," namely, of glorying or boasting; the occasion "that they may be found (a point wherein they glory) even as we," that is, quite as disinterested, or virtually, quite as gain-seeking and self-seeking. It cannot mean that the false teachers taught gratuitously even as Paul (compare <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.20">2Co 11:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.12">1Co 9:12</reference>). Alford less clearly explains by reference to <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.18">2Co 11:18</reference>, &c., where the "glorying" here is taken up and described as "glorying after the flesh"; thus it means, that in the matters of which they beast they may be found even as we, that is, we may been a fair and equal footing; that there may be no adventitious comparisons made between us, arising out of misrepresentations of my course of procedure, but that in every matter of boasting we may be fairly compared and judged by facts; FOR (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.13">2Co 11:13</reference>) realities they have none, no weapons but misrepresentation, being false apostles. <div eID="gen34685" type="x-p"/>
entries.80237231d56fbca371ffb9bc331234b948c4867b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17369"/><div sID="gen34686" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17369"/><hi type="bold">13. For--</hi>reason why he is unwilling they should be thought like him [Bengel].<div eID="gen34686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34687" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">such--</hi>they and those like them.<div eID="gen34687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34688" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">false apostles--</hi>those "overmuch apostles" (see on <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.5">2Co 11:5</reference>) are no apostles at all.<div eID="gen34688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34689" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">deceitful workers--</hi>pretending to be "workmen" for the Lord, and really seeking their own gain. <div eID="gen34689" type="x-p"/>
entries.bcd77b7557dd36eb928faef22d6745630617cb40: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17370"/><div sID="gen34690" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17370"/><hi type="bold">14. is transformed--</hi>rather, "transforms himself" (compare <reference osisRef="Job.1.6">Job 1:6</reference>); habitually; the first occasion of his doing so was in tempting Eve. "Himself" is emphatical: If their master himself, who is the "prince of darkness," the most alien to light, does so, it is less marvellous in the case of them who are his servants (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.54">Lu 22:54</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.6.12">Ep 6:12</reference>). <div eID="gen34690" type="x-p"/>
entries.90104283eccbb20d1039a611b33221dfa8af8c7a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17371"/><div sID="gen34691" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17371"/><hi type="bold">15. no great thing--</hi>no difficult matter.<div eID="gen34691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34692" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">if his ministers also--</hi>as well as himself.<div eID="gen34692" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34693" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">righteousness--</hi>answering to "light" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.14">2Co 11:14</reference>); the manifestation wherewith God reveals Himself in Christ (<reference osisRef="Matt.6.33">Mt 6:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.1.17">Ro 1:17</reference>).<div eID="gen34693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34694" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">end--</hi>The test of things is the end which strips off every specious form into which Satan's agents may now "transform" themselves (compare <reference osisRef="Phil.3.19">Php 3:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Phil.3.21">21</reference>).<div eID="gen34694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34695" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">according to their works--</hi>not according to their pretensions. <div eID="gen34695" type="x-p"/>
entries.ad562661cbe8667ff675af603915a1977f151aa7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17372"/><div sID="gen34696" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17372"/><hi type="bold">16. I say again--</hi>again taking up from <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.1">2Co 11:1</reference> the anticipatory apology for his boasting.<div eID="gen34696" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34697" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">if otherwise--</hi>but if ye will not grant this; if ye will think me a fool.<div eID="gen34697" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34698" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">yet as a fool--</hi>"yet even as a fool receive me"; grant me the indulgent hearing conceded even to one suspected of folly. The Greek denotes one who does not rightly use his mental powers; not having the idea of blame necessarily attached to it; one deceived by foolish vanities, yet boasting himself [Tittmann], (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.17">2Co 11:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.19">19</reference>).<div eID="gen34698" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34699" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that I--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read, "that I, too," namely, as well as they, may boast myself. <div eID="gen34699" type="x-p"/>
entries.e91d9086b64d0df7efde9d14b46a798067f51f1d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17373"/><div sID="gen34700" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17373"/><hi type="bold">17. not after the Lord--</hi>By inspired guidance he excepts this "glorying" or "boasting" from the inspired authoritativeness which belongs to all else that he wrote; even this boasting, though undesirable in itself, was permitted by the Spirit, taking into account its aim, namely, to draw off the Corinthians from their false teachers to the apostle. Therefore this passage gives no proof that any portion of Scripture is uninspired. It merely guards against his boasting being made a justification of boasting in general, which is not ordinarily "after the Lord," that is, consistent with Christian humility.<div eID="gen34700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34701" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">foolishly--</hi>Greek, "in foolishness."<div eID="gen34701" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34702" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">confidence of boasting--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Cor.9.4">2Co 9:4</reference>). <div eID="gen34702" type="x-p"/>
entries.7dbc380d1255f751af1ebcfa535030facb7b9d27: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17374"/><div sID="gen34703" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17374"/><hi type="bold">18. many--</hi>including the "false teachers."<div eID="gen34703" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34704" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">after the flesh--</hi>as fleshly men are wont to boast, namely, of external advantages, as their birth, doings, &c. (compare <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.22">2Co 11:22</reference>).<div eID="gen34704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34705" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I will glory also--</hi>that is, I also will boast of such fleshly advantages, to show you that even in these I am not their inferiors, and therefore ought not to be supplanted by them in your esteem; though these are not what I desire to glory in (<reference osisRef="2Cor.10.17">2Co 10:17</reference>). <div eID="gen34705" type="x-p"/>
entries.cd19a67db8aca8ce697c41fae8ff0b153fefe05c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17375"/><div sID="gen34706" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17375"/><hi type="bold">19. gladly--</hi>willingly. Irony. A plea why they should "bear with" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.1">2Co 11:1</reference>) him in his folly, that is, boasting; ye are, in sooth, so "wise" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.4.8">1Co 4:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.10">10</reference>; Paul's real view of their wisdom was very different, <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.1-1Cor.3.4">1Co 3:1-4</reference>) yourselves that ye can "bear with" the folly of others more complacently. Not only can ye do so, but ye are actually doing this and more. <div eID="gen34706" type="x-p"/>
entries.493d27cb263d27d2725fe53478e18c30e4f9eed3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17376"/><div sID="gen34707" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17376"/><hi type="bold">20. For--</hi>Ye may well "bear with" fools; for ye even "bear with" oppressors. Translate, "Ye bear with them."<div eID="gen34707" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34708" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a man--</hi>as the false apostles do.<div eID="gen34708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34709" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bring you into bondage--</hi>to himself. Translate "brings," not "bring"; for the case is not merely a supposed case, but a case actually then occurring. Also "devours" (namely, by exactions, <reference osisRef="Matt.23.24">Mt 23:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.53.4">Psa 53:4</reference>), "takes," "exalts," "smites."<div eID="gen34709" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34710" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">take of you--</hi>So the Greek for "take" is used for "take away from" (<reference osisRef="Rev.6.4">Re 6:4</reference>). Alford translates, as in <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.16">2Co 12:16</reference>, "catches you."<div eID="gen34710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34711" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">exalt himself--</hi>under the pretext of apostolic dignity.<div eID="gen34711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34712" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">smite you on the face--</hi>under the pretext of divine zeal. The height of insolence on their part, and of servile endurance on yours (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.24">1Ki 22:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.13.25">Ne 13:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.22.64">Lu 22:64</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.23.2">Ac 23:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.3">1Ti 3:3</reference>). <div eID="gen34712" type="x-p"/>
entries.b461c2fc28b39aa3e896fd77512a32bf486fc2d7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17377"/><div sID="gen34713" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17377"/><hi type="bold">21. as concerning reproach--</hi>rather, "by way of dishonor (that is, self-disparagement) I say it."<div eID="gen34713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34714" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as though we ... weak--</hi>in not similarly (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.20">2Co 11:20</reference>) showing our power over you. "An ironical reminiscence of his own abstinence when among them from all these acts of self-exaltation at their expense" (as if such abstinence was weakness) [Alford]. The "we" is emphatically contrasted with the false teachers who so oppressively displayed their power. I speak so as though WE had been weak when with you, because we did not show our power this way. Howbeit (we are not really weak; for), whereinsoever any is bold ... I am bold also. <div eID="gen34714" type="x-p"/>
entries.f981be8b110b290e291aafcc58784b49071fb853: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17378"/><div sID="gen34715" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17378"/><hi type="bold">22. Hebrews ... Israelites ... the seed of Abraham--</hi>A climax. "Hebrews," referring to the language and nationality; "Israelites," to the theocracy and descent from Israel, the "prince who prevailed with God" (<reference osisRef="Rom.9.4">Ro 9:4</reference>); "the seed of Abraham," to the claim to a share in the Messiah (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.1">Ro 11:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.9.7">9:7</reference>). Compare <reference osisRef="Phil.3.5">Php 3:5</reference>, "An Hebrew of the Hebrews," not an Hellenist or Greek-speaking Jew, but a Hebrew in tongue, and sprung from Hebrews. <div eID="gen34715" type="x-p"/>
entries.e421323a884ce84da7c4807a4e95fbe78e5bf76c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17379"/><div sID="gen34716" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17379"/><hi type="bold">23. I speak as a fool--</hi>rather, as Greek, "I speak as if beside myself"; stronger than "as a fool."<div eID="gen34716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34717" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I am more--</hi>namely, in respect to the credentials and manifestations of my ministry, more faithful and self-denying; and richer in tokens of God's recognition of my ministry. Old authorities read the order thus, "In prisons above measures, in stripes more abundantly" (English Version, less accurately, "more frequent"). <reference osisRef="Acts.16.23-Acts.16.40">Ac 16:23-40</reference> records one case of his imprisonment with stripes. Clement of Rome [First Epistle to the Corinthians] describes him as having suffered bonds seven times.<div eID="gen34717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34718" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in death oft--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.10">2Co 4:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.9.23">Ac 9:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.13.50">13:50</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.14.5">14:5</reference>, 6, 19; <reference osisRef="Acts.17.5">17:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.17.13">13</reference>). <div eID="gen34718" type="x-p"/>
entries.9d4d8619ed8761b3a27b4687d9e65f424f68770c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17380"/><div sID="gen34719" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17380"/>24. <reference osisRef="Deut.25.3">De 25:3</reference> ordained that not more than forty stripes should be inflicted To avoid exceeding this number, they gave one short of it: thirteen strokes with a treble lash [Bengel]. This is one of those minute agreements with Jewish usage, which a forger would have not been likely to observe. <div eID="gen34719" type="x-p"/>
entries.c571aea3df6b7dc4b03e3da53a178403f43170a6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17381"/><div sID="gen34720" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17381"/>25. The beating by Roman magistrates at Philippi (<reference osisRef="Acts.16.23">Ac 16:23</reference>) is the only one recorded in Acts, which does not profess to give a complete journal of his life, but only a sketch of it in connection with the design of the book, namely, to give an outline of the history of the Gospel Church from its foundation at Jerusalem, to the period of its reaching Rome, the capital of the Gentile world.<div eID="gen34720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34721" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">once was I stoned--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Acts.14.19">Ac 14:19</reference>).<div eID="gen34721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34722" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thrice ... shipwreck--</hi>before the shipwreck at Melita (<reference osisRef="Acts.27.44">Ac 27:44</reference>). Probably in some of his voyages from Tarsus, where he stayed for some time after his conversion, and from which, as being a seafaring place, he was likely to make missionary voyages to adjoining places (<reference osisRef="Acts.9.30">Ac 9:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.11.25">11:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.1.21">Ga 1:21</reference>).<div eID="gen34722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34723" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a night and a day ... in the deep--</hi>probably in part swimming or in an open boat. <div eID="gen34723" type="x-p"/>
entries.c5b530388a5a090a6ee0499ed66f0478c142caa5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17382"/><div sID="gen34724" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17382"/><hi type="bold">26. In--</hi>rather, "By": connected with <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.23">2Co 11:23</reference>, but now not with "in," as there, and as in <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.27">2Co 11:27</reference>, where again he passes to the idea of surrounding circumstances or environments [Alford, Ellicott and others].<div eID="gen34724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34725" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">waters--</hi>rather, as Greek, "rivers," namely, perils by the flooding of rivers, as on the road often traversed by Paul between Jerusalem and Antioch, crossed as it is by the torrents rushing down from Lebanon. So the traveller Sport lost his life.<div eID="gen34725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34726" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">robbers--</hi>perhaps in his journey from Perga to Antioch in Pisidia. Pisidia was notorious for robbers; as indeed were all the mountains that divided the high land of Asia from the sea.<div eID="gen34726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34727" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the heathen--</hi>Gentiles.<div eID="gen34727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34728" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the city--</hi>Damascus, <reference osisRef="Acts.9.24">Ac 9:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.9.25">25</reference>; Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Acts.9.29">Ac 9:29</reference>; Ephesus, <reference osisRef="Acts.19.23">Ac 19:23</reference>.<div eID="gen34728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34729" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">false brethren--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Gal.2.4">Ga 2:4</reference>). <div eID="gen34729" type="x-p"/>
entries.fa16f288c551a4cf3c81266b3687477ab3f50721: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17383"/><div sID="gen34730" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17383"/><hi type="bold">27. fastings--</hi>voluntary, in order to kindle devotions (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.2">Ac 13:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.13.3">3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.14.23">14:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.27">1Co 9:27</reference>); for they are distinguished from "hunger and thirst," which were involuntary [Grotius]. However, see on <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.5">2Co 6:5</reference>. The context refers solely to hardships, not to self-imposed devotional mortification. "Hunger and thirst" are not synonymous with "foodlessness" (as the Greek of "fasting" means), but are its consequences.<div eID="gen34730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34731" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cold ... nakedness--</hi>"cold" resulting from "nakedness," or insufficient clothing, as the Greek often means: as "hunger and thirst" result from "foodlessness." (Compare <reference osisRef="Acts.28.2">Ac 28:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.8.35">Ro 8:35</reference>). "When we remember that he who endured all this was a man constantly suffering from infirm health (2Co 4:7-12; 12:<reference osisRef="2Cor.12.7-2Cor.12.10">7-10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.4.13">Ga 4:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gal.4.14">14</reference>), such heroic self-devotion seems almost superhuman" [Conybeare and Howson]. <div eID="gen34731" type="x-p"/>
entries.ed7ccc98141f7a47e58574853e76f85cb47a64fa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17384"/><div sID="gen34732" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17384"/><hi type="bold">28. without--</hi>"Beside" trials falling on me externally, just recounted, there is "that which cometh upon me (literally, the impetuous concourse to me of business; properly, a crowd rising up against one again and again, and ready to bear him down), the care of all the churches" (including those not yet seen in the flesh, <reference osisRef="Col.2.1">Col 2:1</reference>): an internal and more weighty anxiety. But the oldest manuscripts for "that which cometh," read, "the pressure": "the pressing care-taking" or "inspection that is upon me daily." Alford translates, "Omitting what is BESIDES"; namely, those other trials besides those recounted. But the Vulgate, Estius, and Bengel, support English Version.<div eID="gen34732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34733" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the care--</hi>The Greek implies, "my anxious solicitude for all the churches." <div eID="gen34733" type="x-p"/>
entries.ddc5f71cb8f12b196e5612663cdf1cbbe85be98f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17385"/><div sID="gen34734" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17385"/><hi type="bold">29. I ... weak--</hi>in condescending sympathy with the weak (<reference osisRef="1Cor.9.22">1Co 9:22</reference>). "Care generates sympathy, which causes the minister of Christ personally to enter into the feelings of all his people, as if he stood in their position, so as to accommodate himself to all" [Calvin].<div eID="gen34734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34735" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">offended--</hi>by some stumbling-block put in his way by others: the "weak" is most liable to be "offended."<div eID="gen34735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34736" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I burn not--</hi>The "I" in the Greek is emphatic, which it is not in the former clause, "I am not weak." I not only enter into the feeling of the party offended, but I burn with indignation at the offender, I myself taking up his cause as my own. "Who meets with a stumbling-block and I am not disturbed even more than himself" [Neander]. <div eID="gen34736" type="x-p"/>
entries.06e511df3b425f27cafe4cc2daaa46f4241184bc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17386"/><div sID="gen34737" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17386"/><hi type="bold">30. glory of ... infirmities--</hi>A striking contrast! Glorying or boasting of what others make matter of shame, namely, infirmities; for instance, his humbling mode of escape in a basket (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.33">2Co 11:33</reference>). A character utterly incompatible with that of an enthusiast (compare <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.5">2Co 12:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.9.10">9, 10</reference>). <div eID="gen34737" type="x-p"/>
entries.0512ed9b009f65282f07a012c46283a1c1d5d625: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17387"/><div sID="gen34738" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17387"/>31. This solemn asseveration refers to what follows. The persecution at Damascus was one of the first and greatest, and having no human witness of it to adduce to the Corinthians, as being a fact that happened long before and was known to few, he appeals to God for its truth. Luke (<reference osisRef="Acts.9.25">Ac 9:25</reference>) afterwards recorded it (compare <reference osisRef="Gal.1.20">Ga 1:20</reference>), [Bengel]. It may ALSO refer to the revelation in <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.1">2Co 12:1</reference>, standing in beautiful contrast to his humiliating escape from Damascus. <div eID="gen34738" type="x-p"/>
entries.32c34e930a9474b41b7113a50cefb5a8d4673c05: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17388"/><div sID="gen34739" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17388"/><hi type="bold">32. governor--</hi>Greek, "Ethnarch": a Jewish officer to whom heathen rulers gave authority over Jews in large cities where they were numerous. He was in this case under Aretas, king of Arabia. Damascus was in a Roman province. But at this time, A.D. 38 or 39, three years after Paul's conversion, A.D. 36, Aretas, against whom the Emperor Tiberius as the ally of Herod Agrippa had sent an army under Vitellius, had got possession of Damascus on the death of the emperor, and the consequent interruption of Vitellius' operations. His possession of it was put an end to immediately after by the Romans [Neander]. Rather, it was granted by Caligula (A.D. 38) to Aretas, whose predecessors had possessed it. This is proved by our having no Damascus coins of Caligula or Claudius, though we do have of their immediate imperial predecessors and successors [Alford]. <chapter eID="2Cor.11"/>

entries.1bb111aea9d3ff6398ac81c22fd3a8ea8b44f68e: <div eID="gen49331" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen49332" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen49333" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen49333" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen49332" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen49334" type="x-p"/> The apostle apologizes for expressing his jealousy relative to the true state of the Corinthians; still fearing lest their minds should have been drawn aside from the simplicity of the Gospel, <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.1-2Cor.11.3">2Cor 11:1-3</reference>; From this he takes occasion to extol his own ministry, which had been without charge to them, having been supported by the Churches of Macedonia while he preached the Gospel at Corinth, <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.4-2Cor.11.11">2Cor 11:4-11</reference>. Gives the character of the false apostles, <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.12-2Cor.11.16">2Cor 11:12-16</reference>. Shows what reasons he has to boast of secular advantages of birth, education, Divine call to the ministry, labors in that ministry, grievous persecutions, great sufferings, and extraordinary hazards, vv. 16-33. <div eID="gen49334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49335" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen49335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49336" type="x-p"/> Would to God ye could bear with me - Οφελον ηνειχεσθε μου μικρον. As the word God is not mentioned here, it would have been much better to have translated the passage literally thus: I wish ye could bear a little with me. The too frequent use of this sacred name produces a familiarity with it that is not at all conducive to reverence and godly fear. <div eID="gen49336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49337" type="x-p"/> In my folly - In my seeming folly; for, being obliged to vindicate his ministry, it was necessary that he should speak much of himself, his sufferings, and his success. And as this would appear like boasting; and boasting is always the effect of an empty, foolish mind; those who were not acquainted with the necessity that lay upon him to make this defense, might be led to impute it to vanity. As if he had said: Suppose you allow this to be folly, have the goodness to bear with me; for though I glory, I should not be a fool, <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.6">2Cor 12:6</reference>. And let no man think me a fool for my boasting, <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.16">2Cor 11:16</reference>.
entries.f992ffc89f9f7266c4d7c597b52aeeb8c0b6a641: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen49337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49338" type="x-p"/> I am jealous over you, etc. - The apostle evidently alludes either to the שושבינים shoshabinim or paranymphs among the Hebrews, whose office is largely explained in the notes on <reference osisRef="Joh.3.29">Joh 3:29</reference>, and the observations at the end of that chapter (see note at <reference osisRef="Joh.3.36">Joh 3:36</reference>); or to the harmosyni, a sort of magistrates among the Lacedemonians who had the care of virgins, and whose business it was to see them well educated, kept pure, and properly prepared for married life. <div eID="gen49338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49339" type="x-p"/> That I may present you as a chaste virgin - The allusion is still kept up; and there seems to be a reference to <reference osisRef="Lev.21.14">Lev 21:14</reference>, that the high priest must not marry any one that was not a pure virgin. Here, then, Christ is the high priest, the spouse or husband; the Corinthian Church the pure virgin to be espoused; the apostle and his helpers the shoshabinim, or harmosyni, who had educated and prepared this virgin for her husband, and espoused her to him. See the observations already referred to at the end of the third chapter of John. (<reference osisRef="Joh.3.36">Joh 3:36</reference> (note))
entries.eca751bfa950ed22122aa7f5682d714421ab6233: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen49339" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49340" type="x-p"/> As the serpent beguiled Eve through his subtilty - This is a strong reflection on the false apostle and his teaching: he was subtle, πανουργος and by his subtlety (πανουργια, from παν, all, and εργον, work; his versatility of character and conduct, his capability of doing all work, and accommodating himself to the caprices, prejudices, and evil propensities of those to whom he ministered) he was enabled to corrupt the minds of the people from the simplicity of the Gospel of Christ; or, to follow the metaphor, he had seduced the pure, chaste, well educated virgin, from her duty, affection, and allegiance to her one only true husband, the high priest, Jesus Christ. And here he seems to intimate that the serpent had seduced the mind of Eve from her affections and allegiance to Adam, her true husband; and certainly from God, her creator and governor. See at the end of the chapter (note).
entries.177f90a2abe56f5b5f4107042e1679dc54a4616e: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen49340" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49341" type="x-p"/> For if he that cometh - The false apostle, who came after St. Paul had left Corinth. <div eID="gen49341" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49342" type="x-p"/> Preacheth another Jesus - Who can save more fully and more powerfully than that Jesus whom I have preached. <div eID="gen49342" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49343" type="x-p"/> Or if ye receive another spirit - And if in consequence of believing in this new saviour ye receive another spirit, the gifts, graces, and consolations of which are greater than those which ye have received from the Holy Ghost, which has been given to you on your believing on the Christ whom we preached. <div eID="gen49343" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49344" type="x-p"/> Or another Gospel - Containing more privileges, spiritual advantages, and stronger excitements to holiness, than that which we have preached and which ye have accepted, ye might well bear with him. This would be a sufficient reason why you should not only bear with him, but prefer him to me. <div eID="gen49344" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49345" type="x-p"/> Others think that the last clause should be rendered, Ye might well bear with Me - notwithstanding he brought you another Jesus, spirit, and gospel, ye might bear with me, who have already ministered so long to and done so much for you. But the former sense seems best.
entries.79c9d23091a883d331e843028d9bf4d63aa457b3: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen49345" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49346" type="x-p"/> I was not - behind the very chiefest apostles - That is: The most eminent of the apostles have not preached Christ, ministered the spirit, explained and enforced the doctrines of the Gospel in a more powerful and effectual manner than I have done.
entries.351fcc8b6042dbbe905c3bf8a801453a30a0befb: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen49346" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49347" type="x-p"/> But though I be rude in speech - Ιδιωτης τῳ λογῳ Though I speak like a common unlettered man, in plain unadorned phrase, studying none of the graces of eloquence; yet I am not unskilled in the most profound knowledge of God, of spiritual and eternal things, of the nature of the human soul, and the sound truths of the Gospel system: ye yourselves are witnesses of this, as in all these things I have been thoroughly manifested among you. <div eID="gen49347" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49348" type="x-p"/> Inspired men received all their doctrines immediately from God, and often the very words in which those doctrines should be delivered to the world; but in general the Holy Spirit appears to have left them to their own language, preventing them from using any expression that might be equivocal, or convey a contrary sense to that which God intended. <div eID="gen49348" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49349" type="x-p"/> That St. Paul wrote a strong, nervous, and sufficiently pure language, his own writings sufficiently testify; but the graces of the Greek tongue he appears not to have studied, or at least he did not think it proper to use them; for perhaps there is no tongue in the world that is so apt to seduce the understanding by its sounds and harmony, as the Greek. It is not an unusual thing for Greek scholars to the present day to be in raptures with the harmony of a Greek verse, the sense of which is but little regarded, and perhaps is little worth! I should suppose that God would prevent the inspired writers from either speaking or writing thus, that sound might not carry the hearer away from sense; and that the persuasive force of truth might alone prevail, and the excellence of the power appear to be of God and not of man. Taking up the subject in this point of view, I see no reason to have recourse to the supposition, or fable rather, that the apostle had an impediment in his speech, and that he alludes to this infirmity in the above passage.
entries.208acdf29a438166707f15c85ec3ec3f089dec2e: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen49349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49350" type="x-p"/> Have I committed an offense in abasing myself - Have I transgressed in labouring with my hands that I might not be chargeable to you? and getting my deficiencies supplied by contributions from other Churches, while I was employed in labouring for your salvation? Does your false apostle insinuate that I have disgraced the apostolic office by thus descending to servile labor for my support? Well; I have done this that you might be exalted - that you might receive the pure doctrines of the Gospel, and be exalted to the highest pitch of intellectual light and blessedness. And will you complain that I preached the Gospel gratis to you? Surely not. The whole passage is truly ironical.
entries.70c2535b5d127bdb22531ed175cffa35dc861f9f: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen49350" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49351" type="x-p"/> I robbed other Churches - This part of the sentence is explained by the latter, taking wages to do you service. The word οψωνιον signifies the pay of money and provisions given daily to a Roman soldier. As if he had said: I received food and raiment, the bare necessaries of life, from other Churches while labouring for your salvation. Will you esteem this a crime?
entries.0edbceca2585054bdb12a6e405190a0c6b23d9c1: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen49351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49352" type="x-p"/> And when I was present with you - The particle και which we translate and, should be rendered for in this place: For when I was with you, and was in want, I was chargeable to no man. I preferred to be, for a time, even without the necessaries of life, rather than be a burden to you. To whom was this a reproach, to me or to you? <div eID="gen49352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49353" type="x-p"/> The brethren which came from Macedonia - He probably refers to the supplies which he received from the Church at Philippi, which was in Macedonia; of which he says, that in the beginning of the Gospel no Church communicated with me, as concerning giving and receiving, but you only; for even at Thessalonica ye sent once and again to my necessity, <reference osisRef="Phi.4.15">Phi 4:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Phi.4.16">Phi 4:16</reference>. See the Introduction, Section 6.
entries.4bef9668bce337500dad101362e0cf5532ef256f: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen49353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49354" type="x-p"/> As the truth of Christ is in me - Εστιν αληθεια Χριστου εν εμοι· The truth of Christ is in me. That is: I speak as becomes a Christian man, and as influenced by the Gospel of Christ.
