there are two oaths, but they are lawful and holy, because they have a good design in view, and a legitimate reason is involved. Hence to condemn indiscriminately all oaths is to act the part of fanatics, who make no distinction between white and black.
“An oath is to be used, when other means are deficient; and more particularly, we are then only to swear, when the honor of God is concerned, or Religion and Christianity is falsely accused; and these are public grounds. To which we may add the good of the Commonwealth: or we are to swear upon a particular occasion to clear ourselves from false accusations and crimes charged upon us, if otherwise our innocency cannot appear; or in the behalf of others, when they shall suffer either in name, life, or estate, and we are required thereunto by the Magistrate, that so justice may proceed.” — Burgesse on 2 Corinthians 1. — See Calvin’s Harmony, volume 1. — Ed.
entries.7c127c573b194e61a961ce2e3a5ecdc2f89739e9:
12. But what I do. He again explains the reason of his intention.
“C’estoit vne fausse monstre de quelque zele excellent, de seruir sans rien prendre;” — “It was a false show of eminent zeal, to serve without taking any thing.”
The false Apostles, with the view of alluring to themselves ignorant persons, took no pay. Their serving gratuitously was a show of uncommon zeal.
“De la resolution qu’il a prinse en cest endroit;” — “Of the resolution that he had taken as to this matter.”
If Paul had availed himself of his right, he would have given them occasion to raise their crest, as if they had been greatly superior to him. Paul, accordingly, that he might give them no occasion of doing injury, did himself, also, preach the Gospel, free of charge, and this is what he adds — that he is desirous to cut off occasion from those that desire occasion For the false Apostles were desirous to insinuate themselves by this artifice, and to detract, in proportion to this, from Paul’s credit, if they were superior to him in any respect. He says, that he will not give them this advantage. “They will be found,” says he, “on a level with us in that glorying which they would wish to have for themselves exclusively.” This, however, is a useful admonition in connection with cutting off occasion from the wicked, as often as they desire one. For this is the only way to overcome them — not in the way of furnishing them with arms through our imprudence.
“Par nostre imprudence et inconsideration;” — “By our imprudence and inconsideration.”
2 Corinthians 11:13-15
13. For such are false apostles, deceitful workers, transforming themselves into the apostles of Christ.
13. Saiquidem istiusmodi pseudoapostoli; operarii dolosi sunt, qui transformant se in Apostolos Christi.
14. And no marvel; for Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light.
14. Neque id mirum; quondoquidem ipse Satanas transfiguratur in Angelum lucis.
15. Therefore it is no great thing if his ministers also be transformed as the ministers of righteousness; whose end shall be according to their works.
15. Non magnum igitur, si et ministri illius transformant se, perinde acsi essent ministri iustitiae: quorum finis erit secundum opera ipsorum.
entries.9ee7554a54eecebb25bd02cb33ccae14a474a773: <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.11.13" annotateType="commentary" osisID="2Cor.11.13" sID="gen122617" type="section"/> <div sID="gen122618" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">13.</hi> <hi type="italic">For such are false Apostles</hi> While he has already taken away from them what they chiefly desired, yet, not contented with having put himself on a level with them with respect to that in which they were desirous to excel, he leaves them nothing for which they deserve any commendation. It was apparently a laudable thing to despise money, but he says, that they make use of a pretense for the purpose of deceiving, exactly as if a harlot were to borrow the apparel of a decent matron. For it was necessary to pull off the mask, which obscured the glory of God.<div eID="gen122618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen122619" type="x-p"/>They are <hi type="italic">deceitful workers, </hi>says he, that is — they do not discover their wickedness at first view, but artfully insinuate themselves under some fair pretext. <note n="834"> <div sID="gen122620" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">S’insinuent finement sans qu’on y prene garde</foreign>;” — “They artfully insinuate themselves, unless one be on his guard against them.”<div eID="gen122620" type="x-p"/> </note> Hence they require to be carefully and thoroughly sifted, lest we should receive persons as servants of Christ, as soon as any appearance of excellence is discovered. Nor does Paul in malice and envy put an unfavorable construction upon what might be looked upon as an excellence, but, constrained by their dishonesty, he unfolds to view the evil that lay hid, because there was a dangerous profanation of virtue in pretending to burn with greater zeal than all the servants of Christ.<div eID="gen122619" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.11.13" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen122617" osisID="2Cor.11.13" type="section"/>
entries.89d4d540871ec7362ce1a7b59ff2184d17e4c66f:
14. And no marvel It is an argument from the greater to the less. “If Satan, who is the basest of all beings, nay, the head and chief of all wicked persons, transforms himself, what will his ministers do?” We have experience of both every day, for when Satan tempts us to evil, he does not profess to be what he really is. For he would lose his object, if we were made aware of his being a mortal enemy, and opposer of our salvation. Hence he always makes use of some cloak for the purpose of insnaring us, and does not immediately show his horns, (as the common expression is,) but rather makes it his endeavor to appear as an angel Even when he tempts us to gross crimes, he makes use, nevertheless, of some pretext that he may draw us, when we are off our guard, into his nets. What then, if he attacks us under the appearance of good, nay, under the very title of God? His life-guards imitate, as I have said, the same artifice. These are golden preambles — “Vicar of Christ” — “Successor of Peter” — “Servant of God’s servants,” but let the masks be pulled off, and who and what will the Pope be discovered to be? Scarcely will Satan himself, his master, surpass so accomplished a scholar in any kind of abomination. It is a well known saying as to Babylon, that she gives poison to drink in a golden cup. (Jeremiah 51:7.) Hence we must be on our guard against masks.
Should any one now ask, “Shall we then regard all with suspicion?” I answer, that the Apostle did not by any means intend this; for there are marks of discrimination, which it were the part of stupidity, not of prudence, to overlook. He was simply desirous to arouse our attention, that we may not straightway judge of the lion from the skin
“Comme porte le prouerbe des Latins;” — “As the proverb in use among the Latins runs.”
For if we are not hasty in forming a judgment, the Lord will order it so that the ears of the animal will be discovered ere long. Farther, he was desirous in like manner to admonish us, in forming an estimate of Christ’s servants, not to regard masks, but to seek after what is of more importance. Ministers of righteousness is a Hebraism for faithful and upright persons.
Beza takes the same view of this expression: “Nec enim illi dicuntur sese transfigurare in Satanam, sed in ministros propos et integros, quibus opponuntur δόλιοι. Hoc enim declarat epitheton justitiae ex Hebraeorum idiotismo;” — “For they are not said to transform themselves into Satan, but into ministers, who are honest and upright, as contrasted with those who are (δόλιοι) deceitful. For this is the import of the epithet, of righteousness, according to the Hebrew idiom.” Another instance of the same Hebrew idiom is noticed by Calvin in p. 196. — Ed.
entries.ff08d1031e1ec8c0b189b5edc9be1a63de939e52:
15. Whose end shall be. He adds this for the consolation of the pious. For it is the statement of a courageous man, who despises the foolish judgments of men, and patiently waits for the day of the Lord. In the mean time, he shows a singular boldness of conscience, which does not dread the judgment of God.
2 Corinthians 11:16-21
16. I say again, Let no man think me a fool; if otherwise, yet as a fool receive me, that I may boast myself a little.
16. Iterum dico, ne quis me putet insipientem esse: alioqui iam etiam ut insipientem accipite me, ut paululum quiddam et ego glorier.
17. That which I speak, I speak it not after the Lord, but as it were foolishly, in this confidence of boasting.
17. Quod dico, non dico secundum Dominum, sed velut per insipientiam: in hac audacia gloriationis.
18. Seeing that many glory after the flesh, I will glory also.
18. Quandoquidem multi gloriantur secundum carnem, et ego gloriabor.
19. For ye suffer fools gladly, seeing ye yourselves are wise.
19. Libenter enim suffertis insipientes: quum sitis ipsi sapientes.
20. For ye suffer, if a man bring you into bondage, if a man devour you, if a man take of you, if a man exalt himself, if a man smite you on the face.
20. Suffertis enim, si quis vos in servitutem adigit, si quis exedit, si quis accipit, si quis attollit sese, si quis vos in faciem caedit.
21. I speak as concerning reproach, as though we had been weak. Howbeit whereinsoever any is bold, (I speak foolishly,) I am bold also.
21. Iuxta contumeliam loquor, perinde quasi nos infirmi fuerimus: imo in quocunque audet aliquis, per insipientiam loquor, ego quoque audeo.
entries.439e3f036250984aeb9e0e47ababc8094d921294: <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.11.16" annotateType="commentary" osisID="2Cor.11.16" sID="gen122643" type="section"/> <div sID="gen122644" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">16.</hi> <hi type="italic">I say again</hi> The Apostle has a twofold design. He has it partly in view to expose the disgusting vanity of the false Apostles, inasmuch as they were such extravagant trumpeters of their own praises; and farther, to expostulate with the Corinthians, because they shut him up to the necessity of glorying, contrary to the inclinations of his own mind. “<hi type="italic">I say again,”</hi> says he. For he had abundantly shown previously, that there was no reason, why he should be despised. He had also shown at the same time, that he was very unlike others, and therefore ought not to have his grounds of glorying estimated according to the rule of their measure. Thus he again shows, for what purpose he had hitherto gloried — that he might clear his apostleship from contempt; for if the Corinthians had done their duty, he would not have said one word as to this matter.<div eID="gen122644" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen122645" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Otherwise now as a fool</hi> “If I am reckoned by you a <hi type="italic">fool, </hi>allow me at least to make use of my right and liberty — that is, to speak foolishly after the manner of fools.” Thus he reproves the false Apostles, who, while they were exceedingly silly in this respect,<hi type="italic"> </hi>were not merely borne with by the Corinthians, but were received with great applause. He afterwards explains what kind of folly it is — the publishing of his own praises. While they did so without end and without measure, he intimates that it was a thing to which he was unaccustomed; for he says, <hi type="italic">for a little while</hi> For I take this clause as referring to time, so that the meaning is, that Paul did not wish to continue it long, but assumed, as it were, for the moment, the person of another, and immediately thereafter laid it aside, as we are accustomed to pass over lightly those things that are foreign to our object, while fools occupy themselves constantly (<foreign xml:lang="el">ἐν παρέργοις)</foreign> <note n="837"> <div sID="gen122646" type="x-p"/> The term <foreign xml:lang="el">παρέργον </foreign>denotes — a matter of mere secondary importance. Thus Thucydides (6:58) says, <foreign xml:lang="el">ὁς οὐκ ἐκ παρέργου τὸν πόλεμον ἐποιεῖτο </foreign>— who did not make the war a secondary consideration. — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen122646" type="x-p"/> </note> <hi type="italic"> in matters of inferior moment.</hi><div eID="gen122645" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.11.16" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen122643" osisID="2Cor.11.16" type="section"/>
entries.844c27f336904f3a89eed1db5da46aeb4c6a6852:
17. What I speak, I speak not after the Lord His disposition, it is true, had an eye to God, but the outward appearance
“La facon exterieure en laquelle il procede;” — “The outward manner in which he goes to work.”
might seem unsuitable to a servant of the Lord. At the same time, the things that Paul confesses respecting himself, he, on the other hand, condemns in the false Apostles.
“C’est plustos afin de lea condemner es faux-Apostres;” — “It is rather with the view of condemning them in the false Apostles.”
For it was not his intention to praise himself, but simply to contrast himself with them, with the view of humbling them.
“Afin de leur abbaisser le coquet:” — “With the view of bringing down their talk.”
Hence he transfers to his own person what belonged to them, that he may thus open the eyes of the Corinthians. What I have rendered boldness, is in the Greek ὑπόστασις, as to the meaning of which term we have spoken in the ninth chapter. (2 Corinthians 9:4.) Subject-matter
Calvin refers here to the rendering of Erasmus, and of the Vulgate. The term employed by Erasmus is argumenturm (subject-matter.) In accordance with this, Cranmer’s version (1539) reads, “in this matter of boastinge.” The Vulgate makes use of the term substantia, (substance.) Wiclif (1380) reads, “in this substance of glorie” The Rheims version (1582), “in this substance of glorying.” — Ed.
or substance, unquestionably, would not be at all suitable here.
“Certes il ne conueniendroit pas bien yci de traduire matiere ou substance, combien que le mot signifie quelque fois cela;” — “Certainly it would not be suitable here to render it subject-matter or substance, though the word sometimes bears that meaning.”
entries.fbc2ec5df6c77c892fcfa5666ccd508719cd5fb8: <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.11.18" annotateType="commentary" osisID="2Cor.11.18" sID="gen122654" type="section"/> <div sID="gen122655" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">18.</hi> <hi type="italic">Since many glory.</hi> The meaning <hi type="italic">is</hi> — Should any one say to me, by way of objection, that what I do is faulty, what then as to others? Are not they my leaders? Am I alone, or am I the first, in <hi type="italic">glorying according to the flesh? </hi>Why should that be reckoned praiseworthy in <hi type="italic">them, </hi>that is imputed to me as a fault?” So far then is Paul from ambition in recounting his own praises, that he is contented to be blamed on that account, provided he exposes the vanity of the false apostles.<div eID="gen122655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen122656" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">To glory after the flesh, </hi>is to boast one’s self, rather in what has a tendency towards show, than in a good conscience. For the term <hi type="italic">flesh, </hi>here, has a reference to the world — when we seek after praise from outward masks, which have a showy appearance before the world, and are regarded as excellent. In place of this term he had a little before made use of the expression — <hi type="italic">in appearance. </hi>(<reference osisRef="Bible:2Cor.10.7">2 Corinthians 10:7</reference>.)<div eID="gen122656" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.11.18" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen122654" osisID="2Cor.11.18" type="section"/>
entries.75cd003915171c5e651fad6fa749c6226fea046d: <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.11.19" annotateType="commentary" osisID="2Cor.11.19" sID="gen122657" type="section"/> <div sID="gen122658" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">19.</hi> <hi type="italic">For ye bear with fools willingly.</hi> He calls them <hi type="italic">wise</hi> — in my opinion, <hi type="italic">ironically. </hi>He was despised by them, which could not have been, had they not been puffed up with the greatest arrogance <note n="843"> <div sID="gen122659" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">D’vne merueilleuse arrogance</foreign>;” — “With an amazing arrogance.”<div eID="gen122659" type="x-p"/> </note> He says, therefore — “Since you are so wise, act the part of wise men in bearing with me, whom you treat with contempt, as you would a <hi type="italic">fool.”</hi> Hence I infer, that this discourse is not addressed to all indiscriminately, but some particular persons are reproved, who conducted themselves in an unkind manner. <note n="844"> <div sID="gen122660" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Enuers luy</foreign>;” — “Towards him.”<div eID="gen122660" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen122658" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.11.19" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen122657" osisID="2Cor.11.19" type="section"/>
entries.eb470080dcd5ba13de8e6473829db51626dc1d20: <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.11.20" annotateType="commentary" osisID="2Cor.11.20" sID="gen122661" type="section"/> <div sID="gen122662" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">20.</hi> <hi type="italic">For ye bear with it, if any one.</hi> There are <hi type="italic">three </hi>ways in which this may be understood. He may be understood as reproving the Corinthians in <hi type="italic">irony, </hi>because they could not endure any thing, as is usually the case with effeminate persons; or he charges them with indolence, because they had given themselves up to the false Apostles in a disgraceful bondage; or he repeats, as it were, in the person of another, what was spitefully affirmed respecting himself, <note n="845"> <div sID="gen122663" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Ce que malicieusement on disoit de luy pour le rendre odieux</foreign>;” — “What they said of him maliciously, with the view of making him odious.”<div eID="gen122663" type="x-p"/> </note> as if he claimed for himself a tyrannical authority over them. The <hi type="italic">second </hi>meaning is approved by Chrysostom, Ambrose, and Augustine, and hence it is commonly received; and, indeed, it corresponds best with the context, although the <hi type="italic">third </hi>is not less in accordance with my views. For we see, how he was calumniated from time to time by the malevolent, as if he domineered tyrannically, while he was very far from doing so. As, however, the other meaning is more generally received, I have no objection, that it should be held as the true one.<div eID="gen122662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen122664" type="x-p"/>Now this statement will correspond with the preceding one in this way: “You bear with every thing from others, if they oppress you, if they demand what belongs to you, if they treat you disdainfully. Why then will you not bear with me, as they are in no respect superior to me?” For as to his saying that he is not <hi type="italic">weak, </hi>he means that he had been endowed by God with such excellent graces, that he ought not to be looked upon as of the common order. For the word <hi type="italic">weak </hi>has a more extensive signification, as we shall see again ere long.<div eID="gen122664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen122665" type="x-p"/>It has been the invariable custom, and will be so to the end, to resist contumaciously <note n="846"> <div sID="gen122666" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr"><hi type="italic">De </hi>resister et contredire opiniastrement</foreign>;” — “To resist and contradict obstinately.”<div eID="gen122666" type="x-p"/> </note> the servants of God, to get enraged on the least occasion, <note n="847"> <div sID="gen122667" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Se corroucer aigrement contr’ eux a la moindre occasion</foreign>;” — “To be fiercely enraged against them on the least occasion.”<div eID="gen122667" type="x-p"/> </note> to grumble and murmur incessantly, to complain of even a moderate strictness, <note n="848"> <div sID="gen122668" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Se plaindre de leur seuerite, en disant qu’elle est excessiue</foreign>;” — “To complain of their strictness, by saying that it is excessive.”<div eID="gen122668" type="x-p"/> </note> to hold all discipline in abhorrence; while, on the other hand, they put themselves under servile subjection to false apostles, impostors, or mere worthless pretenders, give them liberty to do any thing whatever, and patiently submit to and endure, whatever burden they may choose to impose upon them. Thus, at the present day, you will scarcely find one in thirty, who will put his neck willingly under Christ’s yoke, while all have endured with patience a tyranny so severe as that of the Pope. Those very persons are all at once in an uproar, <note n="849"> <div sID="gen122669" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Ils tempestent et grincent les dents</foreign>;” — “They storm and gnash their teeth.”<div eID="gen122669" type="x-p"/> </note> in opposition to the fatherly and truly salutary reproofs of their pastors, who, on the other hand, had formerly swallowed down quietly every kind of insult, even the most atrocious, from the monks. <note n="850"> <div sID="gen122670" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Toutes sortes d injures et outrages horribles que les moines leur faisoyent</foreign>;” — “All sorts of horrible injuries and insults that the monks could inflict upon them.”<div eID="gen122670" type="x-p"/> </note> Are not those worthy of Antichrist’s torturing rack, rather than of Christ’s mild sway, who have ears so tender and backward to listen to the truth? But thus it has been from the beginning.<div eID="gen122665" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.11.20" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen122661" osisID="2Cor.11.20" type="section"/>

21. Nay, in whatsoever. Paul had asked, why the Corinthians showed more respect to others than to him, while he had not been by any means weak, that is, contemptible. He now confirms this, because, if a comparison had been entered upon, he would not have been inferior to any one in any department of honor.
2 Corinthians 11:22-29
22. Are they Hebrews? so am I. Are they Israelites? so am I. Are they the seed of Abraham? so am I.
22. Hebraei sunt? Ego quoque. Israelitae sunt? Ego quoque: semen Abrahae sunt? Ego quoque.
23. Are they ministers of Christ? (I speak as a fool,) I am more; in labours more abundant, in stripes above measure, in prisons more frequent, in deaths oft.
23. Ministri Christi sunt? Desipiens loquor, plus ego; in laboribus abundantius, in plagis supra modum, in carceribus copiosius, in mortibus saepe.
24. Of the Jews five times received I forty stripes save one.
24. A Iudaeis quinquies quadraginta plagas accepi una minus.
25. Thrice was I beaten with rods, once was I stoned, thrice I suffered shipwreck, a night and a day I have been in the deep;
25. Ter virgis caesus sum, semel lapidatus sum, ter naufragium feci, noctes et dies egi in profundo.
26. In journeyings often, in perils of waters, in perils of robbers, in perils by mine own countrymen, in perils by the heathen, in perils in the city, in perils in the wilderness, in perils in the sea, in perils among false brethren;
26. In itineribus saepe, periculis fluminum, periculis latronum, periculis ex genere, periculis ex Gentibus, periculis in urbe, periculis in deserto, periculis in mari, periculis in falsis fratribus:
27. In weariness and painfulness, in watchings often, in hunger and thirst, in fastings often, in cold and nakedness.
27. In labore et molestia, in vigiliis saepe, in fame et siti, in ieiuniis saepe, in frigore et nuditate:
28. Besides those things that are without, that which cometh upon me daily, the care of all the churches.
28. Praeter ea quae extrinsecus accidunt, quotidiana mea moles,
“La pesanteur ordinaire des affaires que i’ay; ou, il y a ce qui m’assiege de tour en tour;” — “The ordinary burden of affairs which I have; or, there is that which besieges me from day to day.”

29. Quis infirmatur, et ego non infirmor? Quis offenditur, et ego non uror?
entries.0645edd214885f0c3c2ed9d3e51067e1955926a7: <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.11.22" annotateType="commentary" osisID="2Cor.11.22" sID="gen122693" type="section"/> <div sID="gen122694" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">22.</hi> He now, by enumerating particular instances, lets them see more distinctly, that he would not by any means be found inferior, if matters came to a contest. And in the first place, he makes mention of the glory of his <hi type="italic">descent, </hi>of which his rivals chiefly vaunted. “If,” says he, “they boast of illustrious <hi type="italic">descent, </hi>I shall be on a level with them, for I also am an <hi type="italic">Israelite, </hi>of the <hi type="italic">seed of Abraham.” </hi>This is a silly and empty boast, and yet Paul makes use of <hi type="italic">three </hi>terms to express it; nay more, he specifies, as it were, <hi type="italic">three </hi>different marks of excellence. By this repetition, in my opinion, he indirectly reproves their folly, inasmuch as they placed the sum-total <note n="852"> <div sID="gen122695" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Proram et puppim</foreign>;” — “The prow and stern.”<div eID="gen122695" type="x-p"/> </note> of their excellence in a thing that was so trivial, <note n="853"> <div sID="gen122696" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Vne chose si vaine, et de si petite consequence</foreign>;” — “A thing so empty, and of so small importance.”<div eID="gen122696" type="x-p"/> </note> and this boasting was incessantly in their mouth, so as to be absolutely disgusting, as vain men are accustomed to pour forth empty bravadoes as to a mere nothing.<div eID="gen122694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen122697" type="x-p"/>As to the term <hi type="italic">Hebrews, </hi>it appears from <reference osisRef="Bible:Gen.11.15">Genesis 11:15</reference>, that it denotes descent, and is derived from <hi type="italic">Heber; </hi>and farther, it is probable, that Abraham himself is so called in <reference osisRef="Bible:Gen.14.13">Genesis 14:13</reference>, in no other sense than this — that he was descended from that ancestor. <note n="854"> <div sID="gen122698" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Qu’il estoit descendu d’Heber de pere en fils</foreign>;” — “That he was descended from Heber, from father to son.”<div eID="gen122698" type="x-p"/> </note> Not altogether without some appearance of truth is the conjecture of those, who explain the term to mean <hi type="italic">those dwelling beyond the river.</hi> <note n="855"> <div sID="gen122699" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Vray est que la coniecture de ceux qui disent qu’ils sont ainsi appelez comme <hi type="italic">habitants outre la riuiere, </hi>n’est pas du tout sans eouleur</foreign>;” — “It is true, that the conjecture of those who say that they are so called, as <hi type="italic">dwelling beyond the river, </hi>is not without some appearance of truth.”<div eID="gen122699" type="x-p"/> </note> We do not read, it is true, that any one was called so before Abraham, who had <hi type="italic">passed over the river, </hi>when he quitted his native country, and afterwards the appellation came to be a customary one among his posterity, as appears from the history of Joseph. The termination, however, shows that it is expressive of descent, and the passage, that I have quoted, abundantly confirms it. <note n="856"> <div sID="gen122700" type="x-p"/> “The word Hebrew signified properly <hi type="italic">one who was from beyond, </hi>(<foreign xml:lang="he">עכרי</foreign> from <foreign xml:lang="he">עכר</foreign> to <hi type="italic">pass, </hi>to <hi type="italic">pass over,</hi>) hence applied to Abraham, because he had come from a foreign land; and the word denoted properly a <hi type="italic">foreigner</hi> — <hi type="italic">a </hi>man from the land or country <hi type="italic">beyond </hi>(<foreign xml:lang="he">עכר</foreign>) the Euphrates. The name Israelite denoted properly one descended from Israel or Jacob, and the difference between them was, that the name Israelite, being a patronymic derived from one of the founders of their nation, was in use among themselves; the name <hi type="italic">Hebrew </hi>was applied by the Canaanite to them, as having come from <hi type="italic">beyond </hi>the river, and was the current name among foreign tribes and nations.” — <hi type="italic">Barnes.</hi> — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen122700" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen122697" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.11.22" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen122693" osisID="2Cor.11.22" type="section"/>
entries.3d4a8fe771c0f61c8f4e1a91d332308826d1908b: <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.11.23" annotateType="commentary" osisID="2Cor.11.23" sID="gen122701" type="section"/> <div sID="gen122702" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">23.</hi> <hi type="italic">Are they ministers of Christ?</hi> Now when he is treating of matters truly praiseworthy, he is no longer satisfied with being on an equality with them, but exalts himself above them. For their carnal glories he has previously been scattering like smoke by a breath of wind, <note n="857"> <div sID="gen122703" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Car quant a leurs gloires charnelles, qui n’estoyent que choses vaines, iusques yci il les a fait esuanoir comme en soufflant dessus</foreign>.” — “For as to theft carnal glories, which were but vain things, he has hitherto made them vanish by, as it were, blowing upon them.”<div eID="gen122703" type="x-p"/> </note> by placing in opposition to them those which he had of a similar kind; but as they had nothing of solid worth, he on good grounds separates himself from their society, when he has occasion to glory in good earnest. For to be a <hi type="italic">servant of Christ </hi>is a thing that is much more honorable and illustrious, than to be the first-born among all the first-born of Abraham’s posterity. Again, however, with the view of providing against calumnies, he premises that he <hi type="italic">speaks as a fool</hi> “Imagine this,” says he, “to be foolish boasting: it is, nevertheless, true.”<div eID="gen122702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen122704" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">In labors. </hi>By these things he proves that he is a more eminent servant of Christ, and <hi type="italic">then </hi>truly we have a proof that may be relied upon, when <hi type="italic">deeds </hi>instead of <hi type="italic">words </hi>are brought forward. He uses the term <hi type="italic">labors </hi>here in the plural number, and afterwards <hi type="italic">labor</hi> What difference there is between the former and the latter I do not see, unless perhaps it be, that he speaks here in a more general way, including those things that he afterwards enumerates in detail. In the same way we may also understand the term <hi type="italic">deaths</hi> to mean any kind of <hi type="italic">perils </hi>that in a manner threatened present death, instances of which he afterwards specifies. “I have given proof of myself in <hi type="italic">deaths often, </hi>in <hi type="italic">labors</hi> oftener still.” He had made use of the term <hi type="italic">deaths</hi> in the same sense in the first chapter. (<reference osisRef="Bible:2Cor.1.10">2 Corinthians 1:10</reference>.)<div eID="gen122704" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.11.23" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen122701" osisID="2Cor.11.23" type="section"/>
entries.9553675289ee2ddf63f60c5367588a2f2291a721: <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.11.24" annotateType="commentary" osisID="2Cor.11.24" sID="gen122705" type="section"/> <div sID="gen122706" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">24.</hi> <hi type="italic">From the Jews.</hi> It is certain that the Jews had at that time been deprived of jurisdiction, but as this was a kind of moderate punishment (as they termed it) it is probable that it was allowed them. Now the law of God was to this effect, that those who did not deserve capital punishment should be beaten in the presence of a judge, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Deut.25.2 Bible:Deut.25.3">Deuteronomy 25:2, 3</reference>,) provided not more than <hi type="italic">forty stripes </hi>were inflicted, lest the body should be disfigured or mutilated by cruelty. Now it is probable, that in process of time it became customary to stop at the thirty-ninth lash, <note n="858"> <div sID="gen122707" type="x-p"/> The custom of excepting <hi type="italic">one </hi>stripe from the <hi type="italic">forty </hi>is made mention of by Josephus: <foreign xml:lang="el">πληγὰς μίας λειπούσης τεσσαράκοντα,</foreign> “forty stripes save one.” (Joseph. Antiq. lib. 4. cap. 8. sect. 21.) It is noticed by <hi type="italic">Wolfius, </hi>that the Jews in modern times make use of the same number of stripes — thirty-nine — in punishing offenders, there being evidence of this from what is stated by Uriel Acosta, who, in his Life, subjoined by Limborch to his Conversation with a learned Jew, declares that he had in punishment of his departure from the Jews, received stripes up to that number. — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen122707" type="x-p"/> </note> lest perhaps they should on any occasion, from undue warmth, exceed the number prescribed by God. Many such precautions, <note n="859"> <div sID="gen122708" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Plusieurs semblables pouruoyances et remedes inuentez par los Rabbins</foreign>:” — “Many similar provisions and remedies, invented by the Rabbins.”<div eID="gen122708" type="x-p"/> </note> prescribed by the Rabbins, <note n="860"> <div sID="gen122709" type="x-p"/> “The <hi type="italic">Mishna </hi>gives this as a rule, (MISH. Maccoth. fol. 22:10,) ‘How often shall he, the culprit, be smitten? Ans. <foreign xml:lang="he">אלכעין חסר אחד</foreign>, forty stripes, wanting one, <hi type="italic">i.e., </hi>with the number which is nighest to forty.’ They also thought it right to stop under forty, lest the person who counted should make a mistake, and the criminal get more <hi type="italic">than forty </hi>stripes, which would be injustice, as the law required only <hi type="italic">forty.</hi>” — <hi type="italic">Dr. A. Clarke. </hi>“As the whip was formed of three cords, and every stroke was allowed to count for three stripes, the number of strokes never exceeded thirteen, which made thirty-nine stripes.” — <hi type="italic">Bloomfield.</hi> — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen122709" type="x-p"/> </note> are to be found among the Jews, which make some restriction upon the permission that the Lord had given. Hence, perhaps, in process of time, (as things generally deteriorate,) they came to think, that all criminals should be beaten with stripes to that number, though the Lord did not prescribe, how far severity should go, but where it was to stop; unless perhaps you prefer to receive what is stated by others, that they exercised greater cruelty upon Paul. This is not at all improbable, for if they had been accustomed ordinarily to practice this severity upon all, he might have said that he was beaten according to custom. Hence the statement of the number is expressive of extreme severity.<div eID="gen122706" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.11.24" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen122705" osisID="2Cor.11.24" type="section"/>
entries.9067750a777a45be123155d43116c14775378730: <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.11.25" annotateType="commentary" osisID="2Cor.11.25" sID="gen122710" type="section"/> <div sID="gen122711" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">25.</hi> <hi type="italic">Thrice was I beaten with rods</hi> Hence it appears, that the Apostle suffered many things, of which no mention is made by Luke; for he makes mention of only <hi type="italic">one</hi> stoning, <note n="861"> <div sID="gen122712" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">Once</hi> was I stoned.” Paley remarks in his “Horae Paulinae,” that this clause, “when confronted with the history,” (contained in the Acts of the Apostles,) “furnishes the nearest approach to a contradiction, without a contradiction being actually incurred, of any that he remembers to have met with.” While the narrative contained in the Acts of the Apostles gives an account of only one instance in which Paul was actually stoned, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Acts.14.19">Acts 14:19</reference>,) there was, previously to that, “an assault” made upon Paul and Barnabas at Iconium, “both of the Gentiles, and also of the Jews, with their rulers, to use them despitefully, and to stone them, but they were ware of it, and fled unto Lystra and Derbe.” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Acts.14.5 Bible:Acts.14.6">Acts 14:5, 6</reference>.) “Now had the ‘assault,’” says Paley, “been completed; had the history related that a stone was thrown, as it relates that preparations were made both by Jews and Gentiles to stone Paul and his companions; or even had the account of this transaction stopped, without going on to inform us that Paul and his companions were <hi type="italic">aware of their danger and fled, a </hi>contradiction between the history and the Apostle would have ensued. Truth is necessarily consistent; but it is scarcely possible that independent accounts, not having truth to guide them, should thus advance to the very brink of contradiction without falling into <hi type="italic">it.</hi>” — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen122712" type="x-p"/> </note> one scourging, and <hi type="italic">one </hi>shipwreck. We have not, however, a complete narrative, nor is there mention made in it of every particular that occurred, but only of the principal things.<div eID="gen122711" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.11.25" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen122710" osisID="2Cor.11.25" type="section"/>
entries.cca86642650201592d94ded071a92b7df465fbcb: <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.11.26" annotateType="commentary" osisID="2Cor.11.26" sID="gen122713" type="section"/> <div sID="gen122714" type="x-p"/>By <hi type="italic">perils from the nation</hi> he means those that befell him from his own nation, in consequence of the hatred, that was kindled against him among all the Jews. On the other hand, he had the Gentiles as his adversaries; and in the <hi type="italic">third </hi>place snares were laid for him <hi type="italic">by false brethren. </hi>Thus it happened, that<div eID="gen122714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen122715" type="x-p"/>for Christ’s name’s sake he was hated by all. <lb/> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.10.22">Matthew 10:22</reference>.)<div eID="gen122715" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.11.26" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen122713" osisID="2Cor.11.26" type="section"/>
entries.3b7ac6e658d4bacdc4b554fcecc52ae004cc5769:
By fastings I understand those that are voluntary, as he has spoken previously of hunger and want. Such were the tokens by which he showed himself, and on good grounds, to be an eminent servant of Christ. For how may we better distinguish Christ’s servants than by proofs so numerous, so various, and so important? On the other hand, while those effeminate boasters
“Thrasones.” — See Calvin on the Corinthians, vol. 1, p. 98, n. 1.
had done nothing for Christ, and had suffered nothing for him, they, nevertheless, impudently vaunted.
It is asked, however, whether any one can be a servant of Christ, that has not been tried with so many evils, perils, and vexations? I answer, that all these things are not indispensably requisite on the part of all;
“Il n’est pas necessairement requis que tous vniversellement endurent toutes telles fascheries;” — “It is not indispensably requisite that all universally endure all such vexations.”
but where these things are seen, there is, undoubtedly, a greater and more illustrious testimony afforded. That man, therefore, who will be signalized by so many marks of distinction, will not despise those that are less illustrious, and less thoroughly tried, nor will he on that account be elated with pride; but still, whenever there is occasion for it, he will be prepared, after Paul’s example, to exult with a holy triumph, in opposition to pretenders
“Des mercenaires;”. — “Hirelings.”
and worthless persons, provided he has an eye to Christ, not to himself — for nothing but pride or ambition could corrupt and tarnish all these praises. For the main thing is — that we serve Christ with a pure conscience. All other things are, as it were, additional.
entries.c5a3c40cad6906969e2d9606e66b09c61ed86e2e: <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.11.28" annotateType="commentary" osisID="2Cor.11.28" sID="gen122722" type="section"/> <div sID="gen122723" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">28. </hi><hi type="italic">Besides those things that are without</hi> “<hi type="italic">Besides those things,</hi>” says he, “which come upon me from all sides, and are as it were extraordinary, what estimate must be formed of that ordinary burden that constantly presses upon me — the care that I have of all the Churches.” <hi type="italic">The care of all the Churches</hi> he appropriately calls his <hi type="italic">ordinary burden. </hi>For I have taken the liberty of rendering <foreign xml:lang="el">ἐπισύστασιν </foreign>in this way, as it sometimes means — whatever <hi type="italic">presses upon </hi>us. <note n="865"> <div sID="gen122724" type="x-p"/> The word (<foreign xml:lang="el">ἐπισύστασις)</foreign> is <hi type="italic">translated </hi>or rather <hi type="italic">paraphrased </hi>by Beza as follows: “<foreign xml:lang="la">Agmen illud in me consurgens</foreign>;” — “That troop which rises up together against me.” He adds by way of explanation: “<foreign xml:lang="la">Certum est enim</foreign> <foreign xml:lang="el">ἐπισύστασιν </foreign><foreign xml:lang="la">dici multitudinem quae adversus aliquem coierit, idque non semel, sed repetitis vicibus. Quia igitur multiplices erant curae, quarum tanquam agmine magis ac magis veluti obruebatur, Apostolus usus est translatitie hoc vocabulo, admodum significanter</foreign>;” — “For it is certain that <foreign xml:lang="el">ἐπισύστασιν </foreign>denotes a multitude that has come together against any one, and that not once merely, but in repeated instances. As, therefore, there were manifold cares, by which rushing upon him like a troop, more and more, he was in a manner overwhelmed, the Apostle, by way of metaphor, made use of this term very significantly.” <hi type="italic">Raphelius </hi>considers the term to be synonymous with an expression made use of by Cicero: “<foreign xml:lang="la">concursus occupationum</foreign>;” — “a crowding together of engagements.” — (Cic. Fam. 7:33.) — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen122724" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen122723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen122725" type="x-p"/>Whoever is concerned in good earnest as to the Church of God, stirs up himself and bears a heavy burden, which <hi type="italic">presses upon </hi>his shoulders. What a picture we have here of a complete minister, embracing in his anxieties and aims not one Church merely, or ten, or thirty, but all of them together, so that he instructs some, confirms others, exhorts others, gives counsel to some, and applies a remedy to the diseases of others! Now from Paul’s words we may infer, that no one can have a heartfelt concern for the Churches, without being harassed with many difficulties; for the government of the Church is no pleasant occupation, in which we may exercise ourselves agreeably and with delight of heart, <note n="866"> <div sID="gen122726" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Car le gouernement de l’Eglise n’est pas vne occupation ioyeuse pour nous exercer tout doucement, et par manicrc de passe-temps et exercice gracieux pour recreer nos esprits</foreign>;” — “For the government of the Church is not a pleasant occupation for exercising ourselves quite agreeably, and by way of pass-time, and an agreeable exercise for refreshing our minds.”<div eID="gen122726" type="x-p"/> </note> but a hard and severe warfare, as has been previously mentioned, (<reference osisRef="Bible:2Cor.10.4">2 Corinthians 10:4</reference>,) — Satan from time to time giving us as much trouble as he can, and leaving no stone unturned to annoy us.<div eID="gen122725" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.11.28" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen122722" osisID="2Cor.11.28" type="section"/>

entries.d78a53c1adc890d9c8f2920c8824a59658d9ac0f: <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.11.30" annotateType="commentary" osisID="2Cor.11.30" sID="gen122742" type="section"/> <div sID="gen122743" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">30.</hi> <hi type="italic">If he must glory.</hi> Here we have the conclusion, drawn from all that has gone before — that Paul is more inclined to boast of those things that are connected with his <hi type="italic">infirmity, </hi>that is, those things which might, in the view of the world, bring him contempt, rather than glory, as, for example, hunger, thirst, imprisonments, stonings, stripes, and the like — those things, in truth, that we are usually as much ashamed of, as of things that incur great dishonor. <note n="869"> <div sID="gen122744" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">De toutes lesquelles nous n’avons point de honte coustumierement, que si nous estions vileinement diffamez</foreign>;” — “Of all which we feel ordinarily as much ashamed, as if we had been shockingly defamed.”<div eID="gen122744" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen122743" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.11.30" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen122742" osisID="2Cor.11.30" type="section"/>

31. The God and Father As he was about to relate a singular feat,
“Vn acte singulier de vray champion de guerre;” — “A singular feat of a true champion of war.”
which, at the same time, was not well known, he confirms it by making use of an oath. Observe, however, what is the form of a pious oath,
“De iurement sainete et lieitc;” — “Of a holy and lawful oath.”
— when, for the purpose of declaring the truth, we reverently call God as our witness. Now this persecution was, as it were, Paul’s first apprenticeship,
Calvin, when commenting on the passage referred to, (Acts 9:23-25,) makes use of a similar expression: “Hoc tiroeinio ad erueem ferendam mature assuefaetus fuit;” — “By this apprenticeship he was early inured to the endurance of the cross.” — Ed.
as appears from Luke, (Acts 9:23-25); but if, while yet a raw recruit, he was exercised in such beginnings, what shall we think of him, when a veteran soldier? As, however, flight gives no evidence of a valiant spirit, it may be asked, why it is that he makes mention of his flight? I answer, that the gates of the royal city having been closed, clearly showed with what rage the wicked were inflamed against him; and it was on no light grounds that they had been led to entertain such a feeling,
“Et qu’ils n’auoyent point conceu telle fureur pour vne chose leger et de petite consequence;” — “And that they had not conceived such a rage for a slight matter, and one of small consequence.”
for if Paul had not fought for Christ with a new and unusual activity, the wicked would never have been thrown into such a commotion. His singular perseverance, however, shone forth chiefly in this — that, after escaping from so severe a persecution, he did not cease to stir up the whole world against him, by prosecuting fearlessly the Lord’s work.
It may be, however, that he proceeds to mock those ambitious men, who, while they had never had experience of any thing but applauses, favors, honorable salutations, and agreeable lodgings, wished to be held in the highest esteem. For, in opposition to this, he relates, that he was shut in, so that he could with difficulty save his life by a miserable and ignominious flight.
Some, however, ask, whether it was lawful for Paul to leap over the walls, inasmuch as it was a capital crime to do so? I answer, in the first place, that it is not certain, whether that punishment was sanctioned by law in the East; and farther, that even if it was so, Paul, nevertheless, was guilty of no crime, because he did not do this as an enemy, or for sport, but from necessity. For the law would not punish a man, that would throw himself down from the walls to save his life from the flames; and what difference is there between a fire, and a fierce attack from robbers? We must always, in connection with laws, have an eye to reason and equity.
Calvin seems to have here in his eye a passage expressly alluded to by him, when commenting on Acts 9:23-25, from the writings of Cicero, to the following effect: “Etiamsi peregrinum lex arceat a muri accessu, minime tamen peccat, qui murum conscendit servandae urbis causa, quia leges semper ad aequitatem flectendae sunt;” — “Although the law forbids a foreigner to approach the wall, no offense is committed by the man, who scales the wall with a view to the defense of the city; for the laws must always be made to bend towards equity.” — Ed.
This consideration will exempt Paul entirely from blame.

4. Quod raptus sit in Paradisum, et audierit verba ineffabilia,

quae non licet

homini loqui.

5. De eiusmodi homine gloriabor: de me ipso non gloriabor, nisi in infirmitatibus meis.

                  </ns0:note> bear with me <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">That which the Apostle here calls his <ns0:hi>Folly,</ns0:hi> was his speak<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing so much in his own commendation; which indeed is no better than folly, unless there be a great reason: which was here; for it was the false Teachers, vilifying his Person and Office, that put him upon it.                <ns0:p n="2">2 For I am jealous over you with godly jealou<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sie <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">

                  </ns0:note>; for I have espoused you to one husband <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">For (saith he) I have been instrumental to bring you to Christ; this he calls an <ns0:hi>Espousing of them,</ns0:hi> (the union of persons with Christ being exprest in Scripture under the notion of a Marriage, <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 5.23, &c.)</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Col. 1.28.</ns0:note> that I may present <ns0:hi>you</ns0:hi>

Joh. 8.43.</ns0:note> the serpent beguiled Eve through his subtilty, so your minds should be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">In all <ns0:hi>Iealousie</ns0:hi> there is a mixture of love and fear: the A<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />postles love to this Church, together with his earnest desire to present them in the Day of Judgment unto Christ pure and in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />corrupted, caused him to write; because he was afraid, lest that as the Serpent by his subtilty <ns0:hi>deceived Eve,</ns0:hi> so some subtil Seducers should corrupt them, and so withdraw them from the simplicity of their Faith in Christ, and obedience to him.                <ns0:p n="4">4 For if he that cometh preacheth another Jesus whom we have not preached, or <ns0:hi>if</ns0:hi> ye receive ano<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther spirit, which ye have not received, or <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Gal. 1.7.</ns0:note> ano<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther gospel which ye have not accepted, ye might well bear with <ns0:hi>him</ns0:hi>

                  </ns0:note>, <ns0:note place="margin">1 Cor. 9.15.</ns0:note> no man shall stop me of this boasting in the regions of Achaia <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">The Apostle often repeateth this, glorying much in it, that in this Region of <ns0:hi>Achaia,</ns0:hi> he had preached the Gospel with<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />out charge to the hearers; he did so also at <ns0:hi>Thessalonica,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Thes.</ns0:hi> 2.5, 6.9. But concerning them, he saith, what he no where saith of the <ns0:hi>Corinthians, that they received the word in much affli<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ction</ns0:hi>; which might (probably) be the cause. It is most likely that he either discerned this people to be more covetous, and too much lovers of their money; or that there was a gene<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ration among them, who, if he had taken wages for his labours, would have reproached him as one that was an hireling, and who did all that he did for money. And indeed, himself seem<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth in the next Verses to give this as a reason.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="11">11 Wherefore? because I love you not? God knoweth <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Can you possibly interpret my not being chargeable to you, as proceeding from a want of love in me to you? God know<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth the contrary.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">12 But what I do, that I will do <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Cor. 9.12.</ns0:note>, that I may cut off occasion from them which desire occasion <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">I know (saith the Apostle) that there are some amongst you, who, out of their hatred to me, would seek any occasion to asperse me to iustifie themselves. If I had (as I might) have taken wages amongst you for my labours, they would either have taken occasion from it to have aspersed me (as doing what I did from a mercenary spirit) or at least to have justified them<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />selves in their exactings upon you. I had a mind to prevent any such occasions of boasting</ns0:note>, that wherein they glory, they may be found even as we <ns0:note n="u." place="bottom">It should seem by these words that some Teachers in this Church, being (possibly) men of Estates, required no maintenance of the People; and would have taken advantage against the Apostle, if he had taken any, Or possibly some others exacted upon them unreasonably; who, had <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> taken wages, would have justified themselves by his Example. The Apostle therefore was resolved to cut off from them any pretence, or occasion of boasting; and to do what ever any of them did, in sparing the <ns0:hi>Corinthians</ns0:hi> as to the busi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness of their Purses.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">13 For such <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> false apostles <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">That is, persons pretending to be sent of Christ, but were indeed never sent of him,</ns0:note>, deceitful work<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ers <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>deceitful workers</ns0:hi>; persons whose work is but to cheat and deceive you: and that, both with refe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ence to their Call and Authority which they pretend to, and also to the Doctrine which they bring.</ns0:note>, transforming themselves into the apostles of Christ <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">They were never A<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />postles of Christ, only they put themselves into such a shape and form, that they might have more advantage to deceive.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="14">14 And no marvel, for Satan himself is trans<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />formed into an angel of light <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">It is not at all to be admired, that the Emissaries of Satan dissemble, and pretend themselves to be what they are not, for even <ns0:hi>Satan</ns0:hi> himself, who is the prince of darkness, in order to the deceiving and seducing of Souls, <ns0:hi>transformeth himself into an Angel of light</ns0:hi>; that is, puts on the appearance and form of a good Angel. He calls them <ns0:hi>Angels of light,</ns0:hi> because they were wont to appear in a lightsome brightness; or because of that glory in which they behold the Face of God; or because of those great measures of Heavenly knowledge which those blessed Spirits have. All tempted Souls have an Experiment of this; for none is tempted to Evil under the appearance of Evil; (Evil as Evil being what a reasonable Soul cannot be courted to.) The Devil therefore, in all his temptations to sin, though his end be to ruine and destroy, yet appeareth as an <ns0:hi>Angel of light</ns0:hi>; moving the Soul to Evil under the notion and appearance of good.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="15">15 Therefore <ns0:hi>it is</ns0:hi> no great thing if his mini<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sters also be transformed as the ministers of right<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eousness <ns0:note n="⸫" place="bottom">It is no wonder if there be like Servants, like Masters: And as the Devil, in order to the deceiving of Souls, pretends to what he is not, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> a friend to them: So those who seek their own profit, not your good, shew themselves to be his <ns0:hi>Mi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nisters,</ns0:hi> driving the same design with him, also do the like, and change their shapes, pretending themselves to be Ministers of the Gospel, and to aim at the good of your Souls, by teaching you the way of <ns0:hi>righteousness,</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Phil. 3.19.</ns0:note> whose end shall be according to their works <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">but God will one day judge of their works, and their reward at last will be <ns0:hi>according to their works.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="16">16 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 12.6.</ns0:note> I say again, Let no man think me a fool <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">I know that he, who is much in magnifying and praising himself, ordinarily is judged to be a <ns0:hi>Fool</ns0:hi>; but though I do so, let me not lie under that imputat<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>on. There is <ns0:hi>a time for all things</ns0:hi>; a time for a man to cease from his own praises, and a time for him to praise himself. The time for the latter, is, when the glory of God, or our own just Vindication is concern<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed; both which concurred here: the Apostle was ou<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> of mea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sure vilified by these false Apostles; and the glory of God was eminently concerned, that so great an Apostle and instrument in promoting the Gospel, should no<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> be exposed to contempt, as a mean and despicable person, or as an Impostor and Decei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ver.</ns0:note>: if otherwise, yet as a fool <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>suffer.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> receive me, that I may boast my self a little <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">But if you will judge me a Fool, be it so; Yet receive me as such while I boast a little.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="17">17 That which I speak, I speak it not after the Lord <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">I do not pretend to have any special command of God, to speak wha<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> I shall now say in my own commendation; God hath left that to our liberty, which we may use or not use, as circumstances of time, place and occasion direct. Or I do not speak according to the ordinary practice of Christians and Mini<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sters of the Gospel; whose ordinary practice is to abase and vi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lify, not to exalt and set forth themselves, according to the more general Rules of the word. Yet (what the Apostle saith) was not contrary to the Lord, or to the directions of his Word; which hath no where commanded us to vilify our selves, or to conceal what God hath wrought in us, and by us.</ns0:note>, but as it were foolishly in this confidence of boasting <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">This my confident boasting hath an appearance of foolishness in it, though really it be not so; for nothing can be truly called Foolishness, which hath a direct and immediate tendency to the glory of God, and is designed for that End.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="18">18 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Phil. 3.3, 4.</ns0:note> Seeing that many glory after the flesh <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">By the <ns0:hi>flesh</ns0:hi> is meant, carnal and external things; which though they be the gifts and favours of God, yet do not at all commend a man to God. The Apostle saith, there are <ns0:hi>many that glory after the flesh</ns0:hi>; and there needs must be such in all pla<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ces, because there are many that <ns0:hi>walk after the flesh:</ns0:hi> now it is but natural for men to boast and glory in these attainments, which it hath been the business of their lives to pursue after. Such there were doubtless in this famous Church; who gloried that they were Native Jews, or in their riches, or in their know<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ledge and learning. Now though (saith the Apostle) I know there is nothing in these things truly to be gloried in, yet others glorying in them, I will glory also; and let them know, that if I thought these things worth the glorying in, I have as much to glory in of that nature as any of them have.</ns0:note> I will glory also.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="19">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:471" />19 For ye suffer fools gladly, seeing ye <ns0:hi>your selves</ns0:hi> are wise <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Ye freely suffer others foolishly glorying and boasting of themselves, therefore do ye suffer me therein to judge your selves wise, and it belongs to the wise to bear with such as are not so wise as themselves.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="20">20 For ye suffer if a man bring you into bond<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />age <ns0:hi>h,</ns0:hi> if a man devour <ns0:hi>you</ns0:hi> 
                  <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">if they <ns0:hi>devour</ns0:hi> and make a prey of you,</ns0:note>, if a man take <ns0:hi>of you</ns0:hi> 
                  <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">If any domineer over you, as if you were their Slaves, or if any bring you into subjection to the Rites of the Ceremonial Law;</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">take Wages of you, and do nothing without hire,</ns0:note>, if a man exalt himself <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">if they carry themselves proudly, <ns0:hi>exalting</ns0:hi> themselves above you,</ns0:note>, if a man smite you on the face <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">nay if they <ns0:hi>smite</ns0:hi> you, you will suffer and bear with such; this is more than to bear with a little folly and indiscretion in me. This is observa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ble, that men of corrupt hearts and loose lives, will better bear with Teachers that will humour and spare them in their Lusts, than with such as are faithful to their Souls in instructing and re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />proving them, though they carry themselves with the greatest innocency and justice towards them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="21">21 I speak as concerning reproach <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 10.10.</ns0:note>, as though we had been weak <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">I speak as to those <ns0:hi>reproaches</ns0:hi> they cast on me; who am by them represented to you as though I were <ns0:hi>weak</ns0:hi> and contempt<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />able: as indeed I am, as to my <ns0:hi>person,</ns0:hi> but not as to my <ns0:hi>Doctrine,</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>Miracles</ns0:hi> I have wrought amongst you.</ns0:note>: Howbeit, wherein soever any is bold, I speak foolishly, I am bold also <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">And being some of them are so confident in boasting what they are, and what they have done and suffered; Let me be a little <ns0:hi>bold</ns0:hi> as well as they, in telling you what I am, and what I have done and suffered.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="22">22 Are they Hebrews? <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 11.2.</ns0:note> so <ns0:hi>am</ns0:hi> I <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">This would incline us to think, that some (at least) of those corrupt Teachers, upon whom the Apostle hath so much re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />flected, were Jews; who had endeavoured to corrupt the Gen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tile Churches with their <ns0:hi>Traditions,</ns0:hi> and imposing on them the Ceremonial Rites of the Jewish Church. Others think other<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />wise, and that the words import no more than this; Do they glory in the antiquity of their stock and parentage, as descend<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing from <ns0:hi>Abraham?</ns0:hi> I have as much upon that account to glory in as they: For although I was born, not in <ns0:hi>Iudea,</ns0:hi> but in <ns0:hi>Tarsus,</ns0:hi> a City of <ns0:hi>Cilicia (Acts</ns0:hi> 22.3.) yet I was a Jew, <ns0:hi>an Hebrew of the Hebrews,</ns0:hi> Phil. 3.5.</ns0:note>: Are they Israelites? so <ns0:hi>am</ns0:hi> I <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Will they derive from <ns0:hi>Iacob,</ns0:hi> to whom God gave the name of <ns0:hi>Israel,</ns0:hi> (from whence all his poste<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rity were called <ns0:hi>Israelites?) So am I</ns0:hi> (saith he) I can derive from <ns0:hi>Iacob</ns0:hi> as well as they.</ns0:note>? Are they the seed of Abra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ham? so <ns0:hi>am</ns0:hi> I <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Will they glory in this, that they are the seed of <ns0:hi>Abraham?</ns0:hi> (this was a great boast of the Jews; as we learn from <ns0:hi>Matt.</ns0:hi> 3. and <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 8) saith the Apostle, I have on that account as much to glory in as they Some here inquire, What difference there is in these three things? for to be an <ns0:hi>Hebrew,</ns0:hi> and an <ns0:hi>Israelite,</ns0:hi> and of the <ns0:hi>seed of Abraham,</ns0:hi> seem all to signifie the same thing. Nor indeed have we any need to assign any difference, it seemeth to be but the same thing amplified in three phrases. But others distinguish more subtilly, and think the first may signifie a glorying in the An<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cientne<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>s of their Pedigree, or in their ability to speak in the <ns0:hi>Hebrew Tongue</ns0:hi>; the second, may refer to the Nation of which they were; the third, to the promise made to <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>his Seed.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>:</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="23">23 Are they ministers of Christ? I speak as a fool, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Cor. 15.10.</ns0:note> I <ns0:hi>am</ns0:hi> more <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Will they glory in this, that they are Ministers of Christ? imployed as the Servants of Christ in preaching the Gospel? I should not boast about this, (in that I may seem to speak <ns0:hi>like a fool</ns0:hi>) but I am much more a Minister than they, both with respect to my Call to the work, and also my perfor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ming of it. I had a more immediate Call and Mission to the work than what they can boast of; and I have done more in that work, than any of them have done.</ns0:note>: <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Acts 9.16. & 21.11.</ns0:note> in labours more abundant <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">I have travelled more to preach it, I have laboured more in the prop<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>gation of it.</ns0:note>: in stripes above measure: in prisons more fre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quent <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">I have suffered more for the preaching of it, I have been oftner whipped, oftner imprisoned, than any of them ever were: See <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 6.4, 5.</ns0:note>: in <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Cor. 15.31. Chap. 1.10. & 4.11.</ns0:note> deaths oft <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">I have been oftner in ha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />zard of my life: he calls dangers threatning death, <ns0:hi>deaths</ns0:hi>
                     <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> (as 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 1.10.)</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="24">24 Of the Jews five times received I forty <ns0:hi>stripes</ns0:hi> save one <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">God, to restrain the passions of his people, which might carry them out to cruelty in the punishments of Malefactors, forbad the Jewish Magistrates to give any Malefactor above for<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ty stripes; (so many th<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>y might give them by the Divine Law, <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 25 3.) But they had made an Order, that none should receive above thirty nine This was amongst their Constituti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ons which they called <ns0:hi>
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> Legis, Hedges to the Divine Law</ns0:hi>; which indeed was a violation of the Law: For that did not ob<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lige them to give every Malefactor, that had not deserved death, so many stripes; it gave them only a liberty to go so far, but they were not to exceed<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> Some think, that they pu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nished every such Malefactor with thirty nine stripes: Others more rationall<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> think, that they did not so, but thirty nine was the highest number the<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> laid upon any. And it is most pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bable, that out of their hatred to the Apostle, they laid as ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ny stripes upon him, as their Constitution would suffer them to do.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="25">25 Thrice was I beaten with rods <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">This was by the <ns0:hi>Pagans,</ns0:hi> for the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> whipped Malefactors with a whip which had three cords. We read of one of these times; and of a second, <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 22.24. when the Captain com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />manded he should be so punished, but he avoided it, by plead<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing he was a Citizen of <ns0:hi>Rome.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, once was I stoned <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Of his <ns0:hi>stoning,</ns0:hi> read <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 14.19. it was by a popular tumult at <ns0:hi>Lystra.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>: thrice I suffered shipwrack <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">We read but of one time that <ns0:hi>Paul suffered shipwrack,</ns0:hi> Acts 27.18. (which was none of the three times here mentioned, for it was after the writing of his Epistle.) But though many of the <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> and Sufferings of this Apostle were written, yet all were not.</ns0:note>: a night and a day I have been in the deep <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Some by the <ns0:hi>Deep</ns0:hi> here, understand the inner prison, men<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tioned <ns0:hi>Act</ns0:hi> 16.14. or some deep dungeon; but more proba<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bly he means, some time when after a shipwrack he might be put twent<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> four hours to swim up and down the Sea upon some broken part of the ship. It refers to some eminent danger <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> was in<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> of which the Scripture in no other place maketh mention particularly.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="26">26 <ns0:hi>In</ns0:hi> journeyings often <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">In Travellings from place to place for the propagation of the Gospel.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>in</ns0:hi> perils of wars <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Through <ns0:hi>Wars,</ns0:hi> happening and being hot in those Countries through which he travel<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ed.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>in</ns0:hi> perils of robbers <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Such as waked to rob passengers by the high-way.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>in</ns0:hi> perils <ns0:hi>by my own</ns0:hi> country<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />men <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">The Jews, who were mortal Enemies to <ns0:hi>Paul,</ns0:hi> whom they looked upon as an Apo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />state from their Religion.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>in</ns0:hi> perils in the city <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">In many Cities where he preached the Gospel, (as we find in the <ns0:hi>Acts of the Apostles.</ns0:hi>)</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>in</ns0:hi> perils in the wil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />derness <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">In <ns0:hi>Wil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dernesses,</ns0:hi> through which he was forced to pass.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>in</ns0:hi> perils in the sea <ns0:note n="i." place="bottom">Storms and shipwracks.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>in</ns0:hi> perils among false brethren <ns0:note n="k." place="bottom">False Teachers and private persons, who cor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rupted the Christian Religion, and were as great Enemies to the Apostle as any he had.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="27">27 In weariness and painfulness, in watchings often, in hunger and thirst, in fastings often, in cold and nakedness <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">The Apostle reckons up several afflictive Evils, ordinarily incident to such as travel in foreign Countries. Of this nature were the <ns0:hi>weariness</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>painfulness,</ns0:hi> the <ns0:hi>hunger</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>thirst,</ns0:hi> the <ns0:hi>cold</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>nakedness</ns0:hi> here mentioned. He also mentioneth <ns0:hi>watch<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ings</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>fastings,</ns0:hi> as voluntary Acts of Discipline, which he used for the end mentioned, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 9.27. <ns0:hi>For the keeping under his body, and bringing it in subjection,</ns0:hi> and that he might the better attend and discharge the work of the Ministry.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="28">28 Besides those things that are without <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">By the <ns0:hi>things that are without,</ns0:hi> the Apostle meaneth, ei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther those Evils which happened to him from persons that had no relation to the Christian Church, but were persons without, (as the phrase is used 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 5.13.) or else such kinds of trou<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bles and afflictions as very little influenced his mind, but only affected his outward man: Such were his <ns0:hi>labours, travels, jour<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />neyings, imprisonment, stripes,</ns0:hi> before mentioned.</ns0:note>, that which cometh upon me daily, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">See Acts 2<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">

                     </ns0:gap> 18, &c.</ns0:note> the care of all the churches <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Besides these (he saith) there lay upon him an inward care and sollici<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tude for all the Christian Churches; and this was a daily care. For an Apostle differed from an ordinary Pastor, not only in his immediate Call from Christ, but also in his Work<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> there lay an obligation upon such to go up and down preaching the Gospel, and they further had, both a power, and also an ob<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ligation, to superintend all other Churches, and to direct the affairs of them relating to Order and Government: And ther<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">

                     </ns0:gap>.22.</ns0:note> Who is weak, and I am not weak <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Who,</ns0:hi> may be either <ns0:hi>what Church?</ns0:hi> or what <ns0:hi>particular Chri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stian</ns0:hi> in any Church? is <ns0:hi>weak,</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:gap reason="foreign">

                     </ns0:gap>, through outward affli<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ctions, or in respect of inward spiritual troubles? and I do not sympathize with that Church, or with that person?</ns0:note>? who is offended, and I burn not <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Who is offended, or scandalized, under temptations to be seduced, and fall into sin, and I am not on fire with an holy zeal for the glory of God, and the good of his Soul, if possible to keep him upright? By which the Apostle doth not only shew us what was his own holy temper, but what should be the temper of every faithful Minister, as to his Province, or that part of the Church over which he is concerned to watch: <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> to have a true com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />passion to every Member of it, to watch over his flock, inqui<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ring diligently into the state of it; to have a quick sense of any evils under which they, or any of them labour. This is indeed the duty of every private Member, but more especially of him whose Office is to feed any part of the flock of Christ, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 12.15. In this the Members of the spiritual, mystical Body of Christ should answer to the Members of the Body Natural, (to which our Apostle before resembled it.)</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="30">30 If I must needs glory, <ns0:note place="margin">C<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>p. 12.5.</ns0:note> I will glory of the things which <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
