                  </ns0:note> concern my infirmities <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">The Apostle here calleth the things which he had suffered for the Gospel, and the propagation of it, <ns0:hi>his infirmities</ns0:hi>; and saith, that he chose those things to glory in. He would not glory of the divers Tongues with which he spake, nor of the Miracles which he had wrought; but being by the ill tongues of his Adversaries put upon glorying, he chose to glory of what he had suffered for God. For as the mighty Power of Christ was seen in supporting him, and carrying him through so many hazards and difficulties; so these things (probably) were such as his Adversaries could not much glory in. Besides, that these things had not that natural tendency to lift up his mind above its due measures, as Gifts had<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> which sometimes <ns0:hi>puff up,</ns0:hi> (as the Apostle saith concerning <ns0:hi>Knowledge:</ns0:hi>) And also these were things which flesh and blood commonly startleth at, and flieth from. That his Gifts, and miraculous Operations spake the Power of God in him, and the kindness of God to him, in i<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bling him to such Effects, rather than any goodness in himself; but his patient bearing the Cross, spake in him great measures of <ns0:hi>Faith, Patience,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Self-denial,</ns0:hi> and Love to God: and so really were greater and truer causes of boasting, than those things could be.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

                     </ns0:gap> 2.5.</ns0:note> The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, which is blessed for evermore, knoweth that I lie not <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Whether this Phrase be the form of an Oath, or a meer assertion of Gods knowledge of the heart, is a point not worth the arguing. If we look upon it in the former notion, it is no profane Oath, because made in the Name of God; nor no <ns0:hi>vain Oath,</ns0:hi> because it is used in a grave and serious matter, and for the satisfaction of those who were not very easie to believe the Apostle in this matter. But I had rather take it as a solemn assertion of Gods particular knowledge of the truth of his heart in what he had said. The term, <ns0:hi>blessed for evermore,</ns0:hi> may ei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther be applied to the <ns0:hi>Father,</ns0:hi> or to <ns0:hi>Iesus Christ.</ns0:hi> It is applied to the <ns0:hi>Creator, Rom.</ns0:hi> 1.25. and to <ns0:hi>Iesus Christ, Rom.</ns0:hi> 9.5. It is here so used, as that it is applicable either to the first, or second Person. The usage of it in these three Texts, is an un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />deniable Argument to prove the Godhead of Christ. The Apostle, in these words, seemeth rather to refer to what he had said before, of his various labours and sufferings, than to that which followeth: which was but a single thing, and a dan<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ger rather than a suffering.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="32">32 In Damascus the governour under Aretas the king, kept the city of the Damascenes with a gar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rison, desirous to apprehend me.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="33">33 And thorow a window in a basket, was I let down by the wall, and escaped his hands <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> hath shortly given us the History of this danger, <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 9.23, 24, 25. Soon after <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> was converted from the Jewish to the Christian Religion, he disputing with the Jews, which dwelt at <ns0:hi>Damascus,</ns0:hi> confounded them by his Arguments, proving Jesus was the Christ, (as we read there <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 21.) This so in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />raged them, as that they sought to <ns0:hi>kill him, v.</ns0:hi> 23. And (as we learn from this Text) to effect their design, they had by some acts or other brought over the Governour to favour their design; (which Governour was a Substitute under <ns0:hi>Aretas</ns0:hi> the King, who was Father-in-law to <ns0:hi>Herod.</ns0:hi>) For (as <ns0:hi>Iosephus</ns0:hi> tells us) <ns0:hi>Herod.</ns0:hi> put away his Wife, the Daughter of this <ns0:hi>Aretas,</ns0:hi> when he took <ns0:hi>Herodias.</ns0:hi> The Jews had got this Deputy Heathen Go<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vernour so much on their side, that he shut up the Gates, keep<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing his Souldiers in Arms. But (as S. <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> tells us, <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 9.24.) <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> coming to the knowledge of this design, though they watched the Gates day and night, yet he found a way of escape by the help of those Christians, who at that time were in <ns0:hi>Da<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mascus,</ns0:hi> v. 25. <ns0:hi>The Disciples took him by night, and let him down by a wall in a basket.</ns0:hi> Two Questions are started upon this passage of <ns0:hi>Pauls</ns0:hi> life; 1. <ns0:hi>Whether it was lawful for him to flye?</ns0:hi> But besides the particular licence our Lord, in this case, had given his first Ministers, <ns0:hi>Matt.</ns0:hi> 10.23. <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> did in this case no more than what Divines make lawful for a more ordinary Mini<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ster, <ns0:hi>viz. to flye,</ns0:hi> when the persecution was directed against him in particular, leaving sufficient supply behind him. The second Question raised is, <ns0:hi>Whether it being against humane Laws to go over the walls of a City or Garrison,</ns0:hi> Paul <ns0:hi>did not sin in this escape?</ns0:hi> But that is easily answered: For 1. This was lawful in some cases. 2. Gods glory, and the good of Souls, were more concerned in <ns0:hi>Pauls</ns0:hi> life, than to have it sacrificed to a puncti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lio of obedience to an humane Law made upon a meer politick consideration.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
